32X	The 32X is a Sega add-on for the Genesis with 32-bit processing power. It can display polygons, which allows 3D games.
32X Add-On	Sega began making the 32X add-on for the Genesis in January 1994 as a cheaper way into 32-bit gaming. It played Genesis games but not Saturn games, and it was aimed at players who could not afford the Saturn.
32X Advertising	Ads for the 32X showed it being plugged into a Genesis console. Together, the two were shown as making an "arcade system" at home.
32X and Saturn	The 32X cannot play Saturn games. Sega said both systems would be sold at the same time, with the 32X aimed at players who could not afford the more expensive Saturn.
32X and Super FX	Sega and Nintendo made early efforts at 3D with the 32X and the Super FX. These gave basic 3D abilities to the 16-bit Genesis and Super NES.
32X and the Saturn	Sega's Tom Kalinske said the Saturn would be priced too high to be a mass-market item. He said the Genesis and 32X would bring volume and keep the category exciting.
32X and the Saturn launch timing	Sega announced that the Saturn would come out in Japan in November 1994. That was the same month Sega planned to launch the 32X in North America.
32X as a transitional device	Sega of America had to sell the 32X while the Saturn was coming out in Japan. Sega described the 32X as a transitional device between the Genesis and the Saturn.
32X Demand	Stores wanted many 32X units when it launched in North America, and Sega could not keep up with the orders. The European launch also had high demand at first.
32X European Release	The 32X was released in Europe in November 1994. It sold there for 169.99 pounds.
32X game library	The 32X has a library of 40 games, including ports of Genesis games. Sega rushed the system to market, which left less time to make games. Sega stopped making the 32X in 1996 to focus on the Saturn.
32X hardware	The final 32X design has two 32-bit central processing units and a visual display processor. It adds this extra power to the Genesis it plugs into.
32X in Japan and Brazil	Japan got the 32X on December 3, 1994. That was two weeks after the Saturn came out there. The 32X came to Brazil in March 1995.
32X Launch Games	Sega promised 12 games at launch, but only six were ready for the North American launch. These included Doom, Star Wars Arcade, Virtua Racing Deluxe, and Cosmic Carnage. Games sold for $69.95 each.
32X names by region	The 32X was sold as Genesis 32X in North America and Mega 32X in Brazil. In most other regions it was called Mega Drive 32X.
32X North American Release	The 32X came out in North America on November 21, 1994, in time for that year's holiday season. It sold for $159.99 and did not come with a pack-in game.
32X Price	The 32X launched at about the same price as a Genesis console. Its price was less than half of what the Sega Saturn would cost at its launch.
32X Processors	The 32X plugs into the Genesis and adds two 32-bit SuperH-2 processors. These are the same chips used in the Saturn, but they run at a lower clock speed in the 32X.
32X reveal and origins	Sega unveiled the 32X at the Consumer Electronics Show in June 1994 as a low-cost way to play 32-bit games. It was made in response to the Atari Jaguar and fears that the Saturn would not be out by the end of 1994.
32X Third-Party Developers	Sega had trouble getting other companies to make 32X games. Top developers knew the Saturn, Nintendo 64, and PlayStation were coming. Many saw the 32X add-on as a dead end and chose not to make games for it.
32X unveiling	The 32X was first shown to the public at the Summer Consumer Electronics Show in Chicago in June 1994.

Bayonetta's Name	Her name comes from a bayonet, meant to show there is more to her than meets the eye. Her birth name, Cereza, means cherry in Spanish.

Blue Stinger	Blue Stinger is a 1999 action-adventure game for the Dreamcast, made by Climax Graphics. Sega published it in Japan, and Activision published it in the West as a launch title for the console.
Blue Stinger CDs and guide	On March 20, 1999, Columbia released a soundtrack album and a single with the image song "Sting Me". SoftBank Creative published a strategy guide with game tips and a developer interview on April 27.
Blue Stinger creature designs	Robert Short created the creature designs and 3D models for Blue Stinger. Nishigaki brought him on through American friends from his university years. Storyboard artist Pete von Sholly was camera supervisor and also made the storyboards.
Blue Stinger development team	Blue Stinger was made by eighteen people at Climax Graphics in Japan and ten people in North America. The North American staff worked on early design and localization. The Japanese team worked almost 24 hours a day for two years.
Blue Stinger environments	The places in Blue Stinger were made with as few repeated parts as possible. They were also designed to look lived-in and realistic. Character movements were animated using motion capture.
Blue Stinger gameplay	You play as Eliot or Dogs and explore the Dinosaur Island complex. You find key items, like key cards that unlock doors, to move forward. Once the two heroes are together, you can switch between them.
Blue Stinger genre and style	Blue Stinger is a cinematic action-adventure game. Nishigaki wanted wit and humor as a theme, to set it apart from the many horror games in Japan. The camera design came from his love of movies.
Blue Stinger Graphics	Blue Stinger uses full 3D graphics for its places and characters, and has many CGI cutscenes. It runs at 30 frames per second because of the many creatures on screen. It does not use bump mapping.
Blue Stinger music	The music was composed by Toshihiko Sahashi, who was asked to make a Hollywood-style score like the music of John Williams. It was his first video game job, and he treated it like a background movie score.
Blue Stinger on the Dreamcast	The team did not know the full specs of the Dreamcast while making the game. Nishigaki said they used about half of the console's graphics power.
Blue Stinger opening and ending themes	The opening and ending themes were recorded with a 60-piece orchestra conducted by Kouji Haishima. They were made to match the finished movie scenes. Only these two themes use CD-quality music; the rest uses the Dreamcast sound chip.
Blue Stinger release	Blue Stinger was announced at the Tokyo Game Show in September 1998 as a Dreamcast launch game. It was delayed to polish the game and came out in Japan from Sega on March 25, 1999.
Blue Stinger staff	Nishigaki produced the game and co-wrote the script. Ayumu Kojima was director, Kazuaki Yokozawa was lead programmer, and Ryosuke Murakami was art director. Masaki Segawa designed the characters and co-wrote, and Atsushi Yamamoto was game designer.
Blue Stinger Story and Writing	The plot of Blue Stinger was the work of Segawa. Nishigaki mostly wrote the banter between the characters.
Blue Stinger voice acting	All versions of the game use English voices, and the Japanese version adds subtitles like a Hollywood movie. Ryan Drummond voices Eliot, and Deem Bristow voices the other lead.

Bullring: Lil Wee Wussy Gap	Lil Wee Wussy Gap is worth just 1 point. On the halfpipe, grind the side with the rollin, jump over the rollin, and grind the halfpipe again.
Bullring: Tight Gap	Tight Gap is worth 1000 points in the Bullring. On the halfpipe, go up the rollin to find a second rollin with space between them. Clear the gap and land on the other rollin.

Burnside pool tips	Skating in the pools at Burnside is a sure way to score points. Be careful entering them, since it is easy to sway left or right and lose your sense of direction. Avoid the small eyeball pool, as crashing there is very easy.

CD-i and Nintendo	Nintendo and Philips made a deal about a CD add-on for the Super NES that was never finished. Because of this deal, Philips had the right to use some Nintendo game series on the CD-i.
CD-i versions	The CD-i came in several versions. Some of these machines were made by companies other than Philips.
CD-ROM advantages	CD-ROMs hold much more game content and cost far less to make, so they are less risky for publishers. Games can sell for less, and short production times mean publishers do not have to guess demand as much.
CD-ROM disadvantages	CD games have long load times and cannot load data on the fly, so they rely on the console RAM. CD-ROM drives also cost more to make than cartridge slots, so CD consoles often cost more.
CD-ROM game storage	Fifth generation consoles began storing games on optical discs (CD-ROM) instead of ROM cartridges. A disc can hold up to 650 MB, much more space than a cartridge.

Doom Forge window entry	Smash any window to enter the building. A Fire Tablet and Health Flask are on the left, and a Spawner is on the right. If your health is not extremely low, enter through the right window.

Dreamcast	The Dreamcast is a home video game console made by Sega. It came out in Japan on November 27, 1998, and around the world in late 1999. It follows the Sega Saturn and is the first sixth-generation console.

Dreamcast Design Team	A team led by Hideki Sato started building the Dreamcast in 1997. The Saturn's hardware was expensive, so the Dreamcast was designed to cost less by using off-the-shelf parts.
Dreamcast Development Costs	Sega spent US$50-80 million on Dreamcast hardware, $150-200 million on software, and US$300 million on worldwide promotion. Irimajiri, a former Honda executive, joked that this was like the cost of designing new cars.
Dreamcast Direct	Dreamcast Direct is Sega's online store. The Dreamcast version of Space Channel 5: Part 2 is sold only through Dreamcast Direct.

Dreamcast downloadable content	Sega was one of the first to offer downloadable content for console games on the Dreamcast. The small memory of the VMU limits how much content players can download.
Dreamcast DVD at E3 2000	At E3 2000, Sega showed a Dreamcast DVD display unit. It was part of Sega's plans for a DVD add-on or a separate DVD unit.
Dreamcast DVD Upgrade	Before the Dreamcast came out, Sega said owners would one day be able to upgrade the GD-ROM drive to DVD. This was part of Sega's plan to let the system grow and keep up with more powerful machines.
Dreamcast ESPN Highlights	The Dreamcast version has glossy visuals. It also includes real ESPN highlights.

Dreamcast games	Dreamcast games include Sonic Adventure (1998), Crazy Taxi (1999), Shenmue (1999), Jet Set Radio (2000), and Phantasy Star Online (2000).
Dreamcast GD-ROM discs	The Dreamcast uses GD-ROM discs, though Sega advertised them as CD-ROM. This choice saved Sega money, but it did not compare well against the DVD features of the PlayStation 2.
Dreamcast graphics	Smilebit pushed the Dreamcast to its limits with bright colors, realistic shadows, and more than sixteen characters on screen without lag. They wanted the game to be impossible to copy on the PlayStation 2, which has less memory.
Dreamcast graphics hardware	The Dreamcast pairs the PowerVR2 with the Hitachi SH-4. The SH-4 is the T&L geometry engine and handles more than 10 million triangles per second. The PowerVR2 is the rendering engine and handles 7 million triangles per second.
Dreamcast Gun	The Dreamcast Gun is the official light-gun controller sold with The House of the Dead 2 in Japan. It has a directional pad and a slot for the Dreamcast's Visual Memory Unit.
Dreamcast Hardware	The Dreamcast uses a Hitachi SH-4 CPU and an NEC PowerVR2 GPU. It shares hardware with Sega's NAOMI arcade system board, which lets arcade games be brought to the Dreamcast faithfully.
Dreamcast Hardware Design	The Dreamcast uses smart subsystems working in parallel, like older Sega consoles. Its parts are closer to personal computer parts than console parts, which keeps costs down. Sega told developers games made for a Pentium II 200 would run on it.
Dreamcast Katana Project	By February 1998, Sega had renamed the Dreamcast project Katana, after the Japanese sword. At that time, some hardware details, such as the amount of RAM, were not yet final.
Dreamcast keyboard and mouse	Sega made a keyboard and a computer mouse for the Dreamcast. They make it easier to move around and use the Internet on the console.
Dreamcast launch in Europe	Europe was first set to get 10 launch games. The launch was delayed from its planned date of September 23, so a few more games were added, for a total of 15.
Dreamcast launch in Japan	The Dreamcast launched in Japan with four games. They were Virtua Fighter 3tb, Pen Pen TriIcelon, Godzilla Generations, and July.
Dreamcast launch in North America	The North American launch had 19 games. Some of the most awaited ones were Sonic Adventure, Soulcalibur, and NFL 2K.
Dreamcast launch in the UK	Ready 2 Rumble Boxing was one of the games available when the Dreamcast launched in the United Kingdom.
Dreamcast Link in Brazil	In Brazil the Dreamcast was sold without the modem because the console was expensive there. The modem was sold separately for R$49.99 under the name Dreamcast Link.
Dreamcast loading screens	The arcade game shows cross-country map loading screens. On the Dreamcast, these map loading screens were made more simple looking.
Dreamcast Logo	The Dreamcast has a spiral logo. A branding agency called Interbrand created the logo for the console.
Dreamcast memory cards without VMU features	Some Dreamcast memory cards have no VMU features, so they lack a display screen, input buttons, speaker and built-in clock. Some hold the same 128 KB as a VMU, equal to 200 blocks.

Dreamcast Modem	Every Dreamcast comes with a modem. Brad Huang convinced Sega chairman Isao Okawa to include it, even though Okawa's staff opposed the extra US$15 cost per unit. The modem is modular to keep up with changes in home data delivery.
Dreamcast Modem and Online Play	The Dreamcast is the first console to come with a built-in modular modem. The modem lets players get on the internet and play games online.
Dreamcast Name	Sega held a public contest to name its new system and looked at over 5,000 entries. It chose "Dreamcast," a word made by joining "dream" and "broadcast."
Dreamcast network adapters	Sega made two network adapters for the Dreamcast sold worldwide, one for dial-up and one for broadband. A third broadband adapter was sold only in Japan. All of them attach flush to an expansion port on the side of the Dreamcast.
Dreamcast online features	The Dreamcast supports online play. It also supports downloadable content, so players can get new game content over the internet.
Dreamcast Online Mode	The Dreamcast version added an online mode. It lets the player display their high score.

Dreamcast online services	Sega spent a lot to build unified online services for the Dreamcast. These services give players more reason to use the console's online features.
Dreamcast PowerVR Graphics	The Dreamcast uses PowerVR graphics architecture. This choice worried Electronic Arts, a longtime developer for Sega consoles, which had invested in 3dfx and was unfamiliar with PowerVR.
Dreamcast price cut in Europe	On 8 September 2000, the day Virtua Tennis came out in Europe, Sega cut the recommended retail price of the Dreamcast to 149.99 pounds.
Dreamcast processors	Hideki Sato's team chose the Hitachi SH-4 processor and the VideoLogic PowerVR2 graphics processor, made by NEC, for the mainboard. Both of these parts have been described as off-the-shelf components.
Dreamcast regional online services	Sega does not have one worldwide online service for the Dreamcast. Instead, each region has its own separate service, built independently by different companies in that region.
Dreamcast Release Date	The Dreamcast version was planned for July 26, 2001. It was moved to August 30, 2001 to give more time to improve the quality of the gameplay.
Dreamcast release dates	The Dreamcast came out in Japan on November 27, 1998. It came out in North America on September 9, 1999, and in Europe on October 14, 1999.
Dreamcast Reveal	The Dreamcast was revealed on May 21, 1998 in Tokyo. Before that, in late 1997, there were reports about a rumored Sega system codenamed Dural that had been shown to some game developers.
Dreamcast SH-4 Processor	Sega chose the SH-4 processor after long deliberation, while it was still being developed. Sega staff said it was the only processor that could give the 3D geometry performance the console needed.

Dual CPU Design	The Saturn was built around two SH-2 chips. Kazuhiro Hamada, a Sega section chief for Saturn development, said one CPU would not be enough to calculate a 3D world.

Dugong	The dugong is a large sea mammal related to the manatee. It lives in warm coastal waters of the Indian and western Pacific Oceans. It grazes on seagrass and has a tail shaped like a dolphin's.
Dumpling	A dumpling is a small piece of dough wrapped around a filling or cooked on its own. Dumplings may be boiled, steamed, or fried. Many cultures have them, such as Chinese jiaozi and Polish pierogi.

Dung Beetle	Dung beetles feed on animal droppings. Many kinds roll dung into balls and bury them as food for their young. The ancient Egyptians held a kind of dung beetle, the scarab, to be sacred.

Dungeon floors	Dungeon floors are randomly made and hold roaming enemies, traps, and treasure chests with items inside. Each dungeon ends with a boss to defeat.
Dungeon order	Dungeons can be done in any order except the last one. Later dungeons have more floors. A dungeon with 9 floors when entered first has 21 floors when entered second to last, with stronger enemies and a tougher boss.
Dungeons	Dungeons are mazes. You guide your party through them to find helpful items in treasure chests while fighting enemies in random battles. Reaching the end of a maze usually means one last boss fight before you can leave.
Duo Team Attack	The Duo Team Attack lets you control both of your team's characters at once for a short time, with unlimited super moves. Some supers do big damage even when blocked, so players try to start it before the opponent does.
Dural	Dural is the robot final boss of Virtua Fighter 3. Her body has a metal surface that reflects the world around her. She drew the most attention when the game was first shown in Tokyo in 1996.
Dural project	An internal Sega team led by Hideki Sato also worked on Dreamcast hardware. The project was first called Whitebelt, then codenamed Dural, after the metallic female fighter from the Virtua Fighter series.
Dushanbe	Dushanbe is the capital of Tajikistan, a mountain country in Central Asia. Under Soviet rule it was called Stalinabad for some years. Tajikistan suffered a civil war in the 1990s.
Dust Mite	Dust Mite is the second car of Rookie rating in Re-Volt. It is an electric 4WD buggy with a top speed of 31 mph (50 kph). It is unlocked right away when you start the game for the first time.
Dust Mite and Pick Ups	Dust Mite weighs only 1.2 kilograms, so it sometimes has trouble when it makes contact with Pick Ups. It is better to dodge them than to drive into them head on, which suits heavier cars.
Dust Mite handling	Dust Mite is the smallest buggy in the game. Its wheels turn very quickly, giving it a narrow turning radius, and its excellent grip means little risk of spinning out. This helps it dodge danger and get through narrow track sections.
Dust Mite on bumpy tracks	Dust Mite can lose control when landing hard from the drop-offs of Toy World 1 or on bumpy areas like Stunt Arena. Slow down before corners, and expect to need more skill than with all-around Rookie cars.
Dust Mite weaknesses	Dust Mite has unremarkable acceleration of 1.97 m/s2, so it is slow to reach top speed and feels sluggish exiting corners. Its small wheelbase gives it mediocre stability, and it tends to stay flipped, much like RC Bandit.
DUX	DUX is a scrolling shooter game made by HUCAST.Net, an independent studio from Germany, for the Sega Dreamcast. It is a horizontally scrolling shooter that relies on tactics rather than fast reflexes.
DUX influences	DUX was influenced by the shooter games Gradius and R-Type. Like them, the screen scrolls sideways as you fly your ship.
DVD	The DVD is a disc the same size as a CD but able to hold much more data, enough for a full movie. DVD players reached stores in the late 1990s and offer better picture and sound than videotape.
DVD marketing in Southern Europe	In places like Southern Europe, where video games are less common, Sony plans to push the DVD feature harder. This is meant to bring the console into more homes in markets like Spain.
Dying and weapons	When a player dies, they lose all their weapons and get the map's spawn weapons, usually the gauntlet and machine gun. They also drop the weapon they were holding, and other players can pick it up.

GameCube	The GameCube is a home video game console made by Nintendo, released in 2001. It follows the Nintendo 64. Its games come on small optical discs instead of cartridges.

GameCube controllers and accessories	The GameCube has its own controllers. Players can also use certain accessories made for the system.
GameCube Development	Nintendo began making the GameCube in 1998. It teamed up with a company called ArtX to design the system's graphics chip.
GameCube development kits	After announcing the Dolphin console in 1999, Nintendo began giving development kits to game makers. Rare and Retro Studios were among the developers who got them.
GameCube game discs	GameCube games come on game discs. You put a disc in the console to play a game.
GameCube Japan Launch	The Nintendo GameCube launched in Japan on September 14, 2001. Japan was the first place where the console went on sale.
GameCube launch games	Nintendo showed its GameCube games at E3 2001, with a focus on fifteen launch games. These include Luigi's Mansion and Star Wars Rogue Squadron II: Rogue Leader. Some games first planned for launch were delayed.
GameCube launch price	Nintendo announced the GameCube launch price on May 21, 2001. It was lower than the price of the PlayStation 2 and the Xbox. Nintendo spent 76 million dollars on marketing.
GameCube motion controls	Nintendo built and patented an early prototype of motion controls for the GameCube. The developer Factor 5 tried them out while making its launch games. These controls have not been released to players.
GameCube name and announcement	Nintendo announced the GameCube at a press conference in Japan on August 25, 2000. Before that, the system was known as Dolphin. In Japan it is shortened to NGC or GC, and in Europe and North America to GCN.

GameCube rivals	The GameCube is a Nintendo home console. Its main rivals are the PlayStation 2 and the Xbox.

Garou: Mark of the Wolves game concept	Planner Yasuyuki Oda changed the gameplay to move away from the usual fighting game rules. The idea behind the game was to make it snappy without getting tiresome.
Garou: Mark of the Wolves joystick directions	Directions are relative to the way your character faces. If you face right, left is backward and right is forward. Movelists assume you stand on the left side facing right, so reverse them if you are on the other side.
Garou: Mark of the Wolves losing to the computer	If a single player loses to the computer, the game is over. The player must continue to rematch the opponent who just won.
Garou: Mark of the Wolves match rules	Each battle has 3 rounds, and both health bars start full each round. Empty the other player's health bar to win a round. Win 2 rounds to win the match and face the next opponent.
Garou: Mark of the Wolves players and controls	One player can fight the computer, or two players can fight each other at the same time. Each player uses an 8-way joystick and 4 buttons.

Gauntlet Legends	Gauntlet Legends is a 1998 hack and slash arcade game made by Atari Games. It follows Gauntlet from 1985 and Gauntlet II from 1986. It was also made for the Nintendo 64, PlayStation, and Dreamcast.
Gauntlet Legends arcade hardware	The arcade game runs on Atari's Vegas hardware. It uses a MIPS R5000 at 200 MHz and an Analog Devices ADSP-2104 at 16 MHz.
Gauntlet Legends bonus characters	In Gauntlet Legends, each player must collect 50 coins to switch to the bonus characters. One player having access to them does not give access to anyone who plays with them.
Gauntlet Legends Castle: Hidden Red Switch	After crossing the bridge, go down the staircase to the west. Just north of the bottom of the staircase is a rock. Break it to find a red switch hidden underneath, then hit it.
Gauntlet Legends Castle: Mini Hedge Maze	North of the hidden switch room is a small hedge maze. The carved stones on the hedge are traps. At the end are a red switch to hit and a gate you cannot pass, which belongs to the other path.
Gauntlet Legends Castle: Quick Switch Bridge	Stepping on a quick switch makes a section of wood appear so you can cross. You must be quick or have a friend help. The bridge will not disappear while something, even an enemy you lure, is on it.
Gauntlet Legends Castle: Two Paths	At the first quick switch near the staircase to the west, there are two paths. If you cross the bridge, you take Path 1. If you do not cross, you take Path 2.
Gauntlet Legends characters	Players can choose from four basic characters: the Warrior, the Valkyrie, the Wizard and the Archer, who is an elf. There are also several bonus characters to play.
Gauntlet Legends coins	Coins in Gauntlet Legends are collected by each player. A player needs 50 coins to switch to the bonus characters.
Gauntlet Legends Compass	You start the game with the compass. It can be toggled on and off, it never runs out, and it is good for helping you find your way.
Gauntlet Legends experience levels	Gauntlet Legends uses experience points to raise a character's level. A list of the experience needed for each level gives the general amount, though the numbers may not be exact.
Gauntlet Legends experience per level formula	The experience needed to reach level n from the level before is 750 plus 250 times floor(n/2). This formula was tested for levels 51 and 99, and the values matched exactly.
Gauntlet Legends home versions	Midway Games brought the game to the Nintendo 64 in 1999. In 2000 it also came to the Sony PlayStation and Sega Dreamcast.
Gauntlet Legends Keys	Keys unlock locked gates and treasure chests, and any key works in any gate or chest. Keys carry between levels, so if you run short you can go back to an earlier level for more or buy them from Sumner.
Gauntlet Legends level 50 experience	Some experience values do not quite fit the level formula. The value for level 50 is one of them, and it looks strange anyway.
Gauntlet Legends level-up pattern	The experience needed between levels follows a simple pattern: 1000, 1000, 1250, 1250, 1500, 1500, and so on. Each step goes up by 250 every two levels.
Gauntlet Legends Mountain Anti-Death Halo	Up a ramp are two locked gates with enemies behind them. Pick them off before opening the gates. The westernmost pen holds a golem and a chest with an Anti-Death Halo in it.
Gauntlet Legends Mountain blocked ramp	If your way at the top of a ramp in the Mountain level is blocked, you missed a switch. Go back and get it before moving on.
Gauntlet Legends Mountain dirt mound	In the second Mountain area, take the route east, not the ramp up. On the north end of the next plateau, a mound of dirt sits between two generators. Hit it to reveal a red switch.
Gauntlet Legends Mountain exit	To leave the first part of the Mountain level, climb the staircase leading up to the west from the landing. At the exit, just stand on the yellow pad.
Gauntlet Legends Mountain first golem	The first golem in the Mountain level waits on the ramp at the top of a wide northwest ramp. He is not that tough as long as you stay away from him.
Gauntlet Legends Mountain first obelisk	In the Mountain level, cross the bridge east from the grassy start area. A red switch on the north side of the plateau raises an obelisk to the west. Walk up to it and it changes colors while Sumner praises you.
Gauntlet Legends Mountain first red switch	Past the lower area, a ramp leads back up to a locked gate. Go through it and step on the red switch. Then return to the now unlocked gate at the far west of the plateau and head up.
Gauntlet Legends Mountain golems	Golems appear several times in this level. One hides with many enemies atop a ramp, one waits in the westernmost pen, and another sits right at the bottom of the ramp past the lava bridge.
Gauntlet Legends Mountain hidden switch	After beating the first golem, go to the west edge of his plateau and hit the dirt pile there. It reveals a switch. Step on it to open a gate you skipped earlier.
Gauntlet Legends Mountain level exit	Near the end, go through a gate, over a hump, and down to a small plateau. Head up the ramp on the northeast. At the top is the yellow pad that ends the level.
Gauntlet Legends Mountain level start	The level starts on a little plateau. A locked gate sits to the northeast and a trail leads east. Take the trail east to a ramp leading down into a little area.
Gauntlet Legends Mountain locked gate	In the Mountain level, stepping on the switch found under a barrel lowers the gate to the north. This reveals another staircase leading up toward the exit.
Gauntlet Legends Mountain obelisk and lava bridge	Touch the obelisk in the eastern pen to hear the voice again. Then head east through the gate to a lava bridge. Past it, beat the golem, open the west gate, and step on another red switch.
Gauntlet Legends Mountain obelisks	In the Mountain level, obelisks hold messages from Sumner. One sits in the northwest corner of the plateau at the top of a very wide ramp. Touch it to hear what Sumner has to say.
Gauntlet Legends Mountain optional west area	A locked gate keeps you out of the west half of the lower area. There is not much there except a key and a barrel. The barrel may give a limited invulnerability, so the trip might be worth it.
Gauntlet Legends Mountain rune	To find the rune in the Mountain level, look for an area of wall that is lighter than the rest. Smash it open, grab the rune, and listen to Sumner again.
Gauntlet Legends Mountain suicide guy	While climbing the northeast staircase in the Mountain level, stay alert for a suicide guy. You will hear him scream before he reaches you.
Gauntlet Legends Potions	Potions are the magic attack and come in Light, Fire, Ice and Electric flavors, which change if you wait. Press MAGIC for a blast around you, ATTACK+MAGIC to throw it, or TURBO+MAGIC for a shield.
Gauntlet Legends story and goal	Players must find obelisks and rune stones to restore the power of Sumner. With his power back, Sumner can defeat the evil demon Skorne.
Gauntlet Legends switch scroll	In the Mountain level, smashing a barrel on the east side of an area reveals a scroll explaining switches and a switch. Switches point in the direction of what they affect, which helps later.
Gauntlet Legends total experience formula	A close formula for total experience at level x is 62.5x^2 + 750x - 750. It fits even-numbered levels exactly and is 62.5 points too high for odd-numbered levels.
Gauntlet Legends Town Cemetery Gate	In the eastern cemetery section, the switch you need is on the east side, south of a tree. It lowers a gate to the north. Other switches there raise treasures, including one under a stump and one in a building to the south.
Gauntlet Legends Town Death Switches	Past the bridge, a barrel to the south holds Death, who stands on a red switch. A guardhouse to the west also has a Death on a red switch. Kill him, or let him die, to reach the switch.
Gauntlet Legends Town Exit	Head north and east to a wooden bridge, cross it, and unlock the gate. A red switch is behind the treasure chest. Cross back, head north, and the exit is at the end of a windy land bridge.
Gauntlet Legends Town Obelisk	South across the bridge from the fountain, a gate closes behind you. Go all the way south to a building with a key inside. The obelisk is on the west side of the building and unlocks the Ice area.
Gauntlet Legends Town Rune Stone	After hitting the guardhouse switch, climb the hill and hit the now-lowered switch on the plateau. Then go back down. The Rune stone is in the hut south of the guardhouse where Death was.
Gauntlet Legends Town: Brown Underbrush Field	This field is full of brownish underbrush that you can walk right through. Walk through it as you head north, because generators and keys are hidden inside. A golem may also be there, depending on your level.
Gauntlet Legends Town: Burning House	North of the brush field is a house on fire. Its locked gate holds food and a scroll, but you can skip it to save the key. Shoot the door on the east wing, then hit the switch inside.
Gauntlet Legends Town: Log Bridge Switch	Head east and destroy the stump just before the bridge, then hit the switch under it. This lowers a gate so you can cross a log bridge. A locked gate waits at the far end.
Gauntlet Legends Town: Red Switch	West of the locked gate by the river bend is a stone pen. In its center is a burned out house with a red switch. Hitting it lowers a wall in the northwest corner, letting you collect the goodies.

Gazpacho	Gazpacho is a cold soup from southern Spain, especially Andalusia. It is usually made from raw blended tomatoes, peppers, cucumber, garlic, olive oil, vinegar, and bread. It is a popular dish in hot summer weather.
GD-ROM	The GD-ROM, short for gigabyte disc read-only memory, is a special optical disc format. Sega and Yamaha made it together for the Dreamcast and other Sega systems.
GD-ROM and Piracy	The extra space and new format were also meant to help stop game copying. Piracy was a big worry for CD-based consoles, and it was very common on the PlayStation.
GD-ROM Disc Layout	A GD-ROM has a single-density track near the center of the disc. Around it is a double-density track, which holds most of the disc's space.
GD-ROM Discs	Dreamcast games come on the GD-ROM disc format. Sega chose this format to avoid the cost of paying for DVD licensing.
GD-ROM Drive Speed	The GD-ROM drive in the Dreamcast reads data in constant angular velocity (CAV) mode. It can read at speeds of up to 12x.
GD-ROM for Sega NAOMI	GD-ROM was offered as an upgrade for Sega NAOMI, the arcade cousin of the Dreamcast, and for Sega NAOMI 2. It gives these arcade systems another kind of media besides their usual game cartridges.
GD-ROM security	The Dreamcast was seen as one of the most secure consoles because it used the GD-ROM. Its main protection was a scrambled EXE file on the disc, which the console unscrambled in memory when a GD-ROM was inserted.
GD-ROM Storage Size	A GD-ROM can hold up to 1 GB of data. It is a double-density format based on the CD-ROM, which usually holds about 650 MB.
GD-ROM vs DVD-ROM	DVD-ROM could also have given more space. But it was new technology at the time, and using it would have made the console cost too much to build.

Genesis and Atari	Sega offered Atari Corporation the rights to market the Genesis in North America. David Rosen made the offer to Atari CEO Jack Tramiel and Michael Katz. Tramiel said no because he felt it was too expensive, and Atari focused on the Atari ST instead.
Genesis does what Nintendon't	"Genesis does what Nintendon't" was a Sega slogan made under Michael Katz. It was part of his plan to show that the Genesis could do arcade-like games better than the NES with its simpler 8-bit graphics.
Genesis Hardware	The Genesis was based on Sega's System 16 arcade board. It uses a Motorola 68000 as its main processor and a Zilog Z80 to control sound. Its video system supports hardware sprites, tiles, and scrolling.

Genesis Main Processor	The Genesis uses a Motorola 68000 as its main CPU, which made it a 16-bit system. Its design was adapted from Sega's System 16 arcade board.
Genesis Name	In North America, the Mega Drive was renamed Genesis. Rosen insisted on the name because he disliked Mega Drive and wanted it to stand for a new beginning for Sega.
Genesis Nomad	The Genesis Nomad is a portable version of the Genesis, released by Sega in 1995. It was meant to work alongside the Game Gear, not replace it. Sega said the two systems could co-exist.
Genesis North American Launch	Sega launched the Genesis in North America through its own company, Sega of America. It officially launched in September 1989. A few units reached stores in New York and Los Angeles in late August.
Genesis Release Dates	Sega released the console in Japan in October 1988 as the Mega Drive. It came to North America in August 1989 as the Genesis. In 1990 it reached Europe, Australasia, and Brazil.
Genesis Sound Chip	A Zilog Z80 is used as a second CPU just for sound. Sega worried the main CPU would have too much work if it handled both the visuals and the audio.
Genesis US launch	Sega of America gave the Genesis a limited launch in August 1989 in test markets in New York City and Los Angeles. The launch system came bundled with Altered Beast, a game first made for arcades.

GunLord Death Warps	In GunLord you can teleport back by dying on purpose. The game respawns you at the last place you stood upright on solid ground, so you can abuse this to warp back.
GunLord Diamonds Counter	The GunLord HUD has a Diamonds counter that tracks the diamonds you pick up. The counter turns green once you have collected all of them.
GunLord easy mode	The easy mode is best for beginners learning the game. It has many Extends and no time limit, and you can keep continuing from the spot where you died.
GunLord Extends in Arcade mode	In Arcade mode, Extends are replaced by Time Extends. The number needed for 100% does not change, even in levels that have extra Time Extends.
GunLord game clear bonus	The game clear bonus is only given after the last stage. It is worth 100,000 points, plus 5,000 points for every life you have left.
GunLord game modes	The first screen of GunLord lets you choose between two modes. One is an easy mode for beginners, and the other is a harder mode for experienced players.
GunLord gameplay style	GunLord plays like Turrican. The player explores waste lands and blasts enemies along the way.
GunLord hard mode timer	The harder mode removes the intro cutscene and adds a timer. You can add time by collecting Diamonds and Time Extend items, which replace the One Up items.
GunLord Health Points	The HUD in GunLord shows your Health Points. If your Health Points go down to 0, you lose a life.
GunLord Hiscore Table	A high enough score can be entered in the Hiscore Table. It lists rank, score, time, completion rate, Big Diamonds, stage and name. Arcade mode scores have a red A in front.
GunLord Hiscore Table colors	In the Hiscore Table, the line in red is the score you just entered. A line in green means that player cleared the game.
GunLord Low% category	In Low%, the goal is to finish as fast as possible with the lowest completion rate. That lowest rate is still unknown, and no run is known yet in this category.

GunLord scoring	GunLord has no real scoring system. The only way to get points is to defeat enemies, and the score is capped at 655,350 points.

How dial-up modems work	A dial-up connection uses modems. The modem turns audio signals into data for a computer or router. It also turns data from those devices into signals sent to another modem at the ISP.
How dial-up works	Dial-up Internet access uses audio signals over a telephone line. A modem turns the computer's digital data into sound and sends it to another modem, which turns it back into digital data.

How much pre-compression helps	Pre-compression works much better than the on-the-fly compression in V.44 modems. Website text is usually shrunk to 5 percent, for about 1000 kbit/s effective speed. JPEG, GIF and PNG images shrink to 15 to 20 percent, for up to 300 kbit/s.

How PowerVR draws a frame	PowerVR usually waits until it has all the triangles for a frame before drawing. Texturing and shading of pixels are put off until the chip knows which surface is visible at each pixel.
How PowerVR draws pixels	PowerVR renders tiles using a process similar to ray-casting. Rays are simulated as if cast onto the triangles of the tile, and each pixel comes from the triangle closest to the camera.
How PowerVR PC Cards Work	Early PowerVR cards are 3D-only boards. They use the memory of your main 2D video card as the framebuffer over PCI. In theory this allows much higher 3D resolutions, especially in PowerSGL games.
How Q*bert Got Its Name	The game was called Cubes during most of its making. In a meeting, someone suggested Hubert, and a staff member mixed Cubes and Hubert into Cubert. Art director Richard Tracy changed it to Q-bert, and the hyphen later became an asterisk.
How races work	In Redline Racer you control a motorcycle racer. You start every race from the last position, and each race lasts for three laps.
How Resident Evil 3 became the third main game	Resident Evil 3 began as a spin-off side project. Capcom did not want fans to wait years for a new Resident Evil on PlayStation, so it promoted this project to be the third main game.
How Rez began	The idea for Rez came around 1994 to 1995. While in Europe for Sega Rally Championship 2, Mizuguchi saw crowds swaying to music at the Street Parade. He wanted to make that kind of game.
How Samba de Amigo was made	Samba de Amigo began as an experimental arcade game, made quickly by a team with little game-making experience. Director Shun Nakamura wanted players to have fun performing music, not just playing it.
How Sega Started Making Games	Sega imported used machines that broke often and needed repairs. The company had to build new guns, flippers, and other parts for them. Former Sega director Akira Nagai said this is what led Sega to make its own games.
How Shadow Man Was Made	Acclaim Studios Teesside first built the game engine with no set idea in mind. Acclaim Entertainment then offered about eight comic book series to base a game on, and the team picked Shadow Man. The budget was over $6 million.
How Sonic was chosen	Ohshima and Naka already had a game and character ready. Ohshima said their team was the only one to put in so much time and effort, which helped Sega pick their idea.
How Sonic Was Created	Sega wanted a flagship series to compete with Nintendo's Mario series. Its research and development department submitted several character designs. A spiky teal hedgehog was finally picked as Sega's new mascot.
How Space Channel 5 began	Sega asked Tetsuya Mizuguchi to make a Dreamcast game for female casual players. He talked with young girls about their tastes and found they liked straight puzzle games. The idea began in 1993, and full work started in 1998.
How SSS penalties grow	SSS looks at a window of 16 moves. The first two uses of a move are normal. On the third use, three frames of blockstun are taken away, and each later use takes one more frame.
How the game plays	Real Sound plays like a visual novel, but the screen stays blank. You mostly listen as the story unfolds. When a set of chimes rings, you must make a choice, and your choices change how the story goes.
How the game was made	Sega chairman Isao Okawa believed online play was the future and asked Sonic Team to make an online Dreamcast game. Yuji Naka produced it, and the team took ideas from Diablo and from their work on ChuChu Rocket!.
How the game was started	Activision saw skateboarding games like Top Skater and Street Sk8er as a growing market for young players. Another studio first tried to make the game, but Activision was not impressed, so the project went to Neversoft.
How the MIL-CD flaw works	When the Dreamcast loads from an MIL-CD, the EXE file goes straight into memory without being unscrambled. This skips the copy protection used on GD-ROM discs.
How the sisters address their brother	Each sister has her own special way of saying older brother. Every name comes from onii-san or ani, which both mean older brother. Most of these names are rarely or never used in Japan.

Hydro Thunder arcade cabinet	The arcade cabinet is based on Midway's Hyperdrive and was also sold as a conversion kit for it. It uses the seat from Atari's San Francisco Rush and the steering wheel from Cruis'n USA, without foot pedals.

Hydro Thunder bonus boats	Bonus boats in Hydro Thunder are unlocked by entering a combination. They are very hard to control and are a little more offbeat than the other boats in the game.
Hydro Thunder boost on circuit tracks	Use checkpoint times to compare your runs. On circuit tracks, do not overuse boost early for better split times, or you will have little or no boost left on the last lap.
Hydro Thunder boost super start	Hold brake or boost when the track appears. Switch to accelerate as the 3 fades, back to brake/boost as the 2 fades, then accelerate as the 1 fades. This gives a jump start plus a 4 second boost.
Hydro Thunder cornering	Take a longer, wider path through turns and avoid sharp turns. The less the boat turns at high speed, the less speed you lose. This is called a racing line, just like in road racing games.
Hydro Thunder home versions	Hydro Thunder started in the arcade. It was also made for home consoles, including the PlayStation, the Dreamcast, and the Nintendo 64.
Hydro Thunder hydro jump	Press accelerate, then brake, then boost, letting go of each in turn. Overlapping the brake to boost switch works better, and a longer overlap gives a higher jump. It is needed to win harder tracks.
Hydro Thunder on Dreamcast	The Dreamcast version of Hydro Thunder is a port of the arcade game. It brings home the same graphics, boats and courses that players found in the arcade.

Hydro Thunder ramps	Avoid hitting anything unless it is a ramp. On ramps with arrows, try to hit only one side while following the arrows to gain speed. Longer and flatter ramps give a bigger speed increase.
Hydro Thunder speed in the air	After a hydro jump, use boosts to reach maximum speed in the air. Once at top speed, let go of boost. You keep that speed until you land or hit something.

Ikaruga Chaining and Survival	In Ikaruga, it is not uncommon for a chain-focused strategy to also give you the best chance of basic survival. Playing for chains can help you stay alive.
Ikaruga Chapter One 3x6 columns	Two groups come down as 3x6 columns, white on the left and black on the right. They briefly form a 6x6 square, then slowly move apart. Hold fire and cut through them quickly, and later learn to chain each color separately.
Ikaruga Chapter One bonus enemies	If you clear the columns quickly enough, 1 or 2 groups of 3 small bonus ships appear from the top corners. They do not shoot, so they are easy targets if you are ready to fire.
Ikaruga Chapter One chaining	The first section of Chapter One allows 22 chains in total, and two of them are bonus rows that need fast play. To save time, keep your ship moving upward as you kill the second 3x6 group.
Ikaruga Chapter One first section enemies	The first section of Chapter One is short and simple. It has 60 enemies in 6 groups. The first four groups come in turns from the upper-right and left-hand corners, and each enemy needs only one shot.
Ikaruga Chapter One name	Chapter One of Ikaruga is called IDEAL. It may have this name because it is easy, straightforward and very neatly ordered. The chapter has five parts, and the last part is a timed boss fight.
Ikaruga Chapter One polarity tip	In the first section of Chapter One, your polarity does not matter, so you can stay one color the whole time. New players should still practice switching between white and black to get the hang of it.
Ikaruga chapters	Ikaruga is split into Chapter 1, Chapter 2, Chapter 3, Chapter 4 and a Final Chapter. Each chapter can be played in any mode. You get a grade when you complete one, and A or better is a top result.
Ikaruga development start	Work on Ikaruga began while Treasure was still making Sin and Punishment. The game was self-funded by Treasure. Because company resources went to Sin and Punishment, director Hiroshi Iuchi worked on Ikaruga at home in his spare time.

Ikaruga Polarity Switching	The Ikaruga is the first fighter built that uses both energy polarities. It can successfully switch between the two polarities.
Ikaruga prototype	Director Hiroshi Iuchi built the first prototype of Ikaruga with help from programmer Atsutomo Nakagawa. To finish it quickly, Iuchi reused sprites from Radiant Silvergun, an earlier Treasure shooter.
Ikaruga Stage 1 Hrz2 Demo	If you need a strategy for section two of Ikaruga Stage 1, watch the Hrz2 demo. It shows a way to handle the enemy pattern in this part of the stage.
Ikaruga Stage 1 Section Two	Section two of Ikaruga Stage 1 is pretty straightforward. Once you have memorized the enemy pattern, it should not be much of a problem to survive and get a max chain.
Ikaruga Stage 1 Section Two Enemy Group	Section two of Stage 1 has one group of 6 enemies with alternating polarity. These ships have heavier guns than the enemies before them, so take them out quickly.

KYRO 16-bit quality	KYRO gives very good 16-bit image quality. It renders into its internal 32-bit tile cache, then scales down to 16-bit. This can help speed when memory bandwidth is short, without losing much image quality.
KYRO driver settings	Because its design is unusual, KYRO can sometimes show problems like missing geometry in games. The driver has many compatibility settings, such as turning off the internal Z-buffer, but these can slow performance.
KYRO features	KYRO chips support 8-layer multitexturing, Environment Mapped Bump Mapping, Full Scene Anti-Aliasing, and Trilinear and Anisotropic filtering. The KYRO II can do Dot3 Bump Mapping at about the same speed as a GeForce 2 GTS.
KYRO II	The STM PowerVR3 KYRO II is a 2001 refresh of the KYRO. It likely has a longer pipeline to reach higher clock speeds. In some benchmarks it can rival the pricier ATI Radeon DDR and NVIDIA GeForce 2 GTS.
KYRO II SE	The STG4800 KYRO II SE is a planned second refresh of the KYRO card. Besides a faster clockspeed, it was announced with EnT&L, a software emulation of hardware T&L.
KYRO III	The STG5500 KYRO III is based on the next-generation PowerVR4 design. Unlike earlier KYRO cards, it includes hardware T&L.
KYRO missing features	KYRO chips lack hardware transform and lighting, Cube Environment Mapping, and old 8-bit paletted textures. For texture compression, only the common DXT1 format works. The PowerSGL API is no longer supported.
L'Anse aux Meadows	L'Anse aux Meadows is a site in Newfoundland, Canada, where Norse people lived around the year 1000. It was found in 1960. It is the only proven Norse settlement in North America and a World Heritage Site.

Lacrosse	Lacrosse is a team sport in which players use sticks with small nets to catch, carry, and throw a ball into a goal. The game was first played by Native American peoples. It is popular in North America.
Ladybug	Ladybugs are small, round beetles, often red or orange with black spots. They eat aphids and other plant pests, so many gardeners and farmers welcome them. Their bright colors warn birds that they taste bad.

Lake Powell 9 second boost	In some versions of the game, you can see a distant bridge in Lake Powell with a 9 second boost. Skip the 4 second boosts, because the 9 second boost is the one you want.
Lake Powell boats	Around the first sharp left is a boat, so stay to its right and grab the 4 second boost ahead. Later, an even sharper left has a boat on the right side that can easily get in the way.
Lake Powell bridge ramp	To reach the 9 second boost in Lake Powell, head straight at the middle of the archway bridge, where there is a ramp. Boost up the ramp to get an extra jump and fly toward the 9 second boost.
Lake Powell bridge with archways	Past the checkpoint and a right-hand turn in Lake Powell, there is a bridge with two large archways. Each archway holds a 4 second boost.
Lake Powell cavern split	In the tunnel cavern, a rock sits in the middle of the track. The left has a 4 second boost and the right has a 9 second boost, so stick to the right.
Lake Powell finish	Right after the 4 second boosts in Lake Powell is a left-hand turn toward the finish. The ramp there does not really matter, since you should have enough boost left to bounce your way to the end.
Lake Powell first straightaway	After flying over the archway with the 9 second boost, head down the straightaway. Do not boost all the way down it, because there is a sharp left turn at the end.
Lake Powell hanging boost	Near the end of a short tunnel stretch, a 4 second boost hangs in the air just before a left turn. Jump early so you are on your way down when you get it.
Lake Powell hanging boost tip	After the helicopter jump in Lake Powell, a left turn has a hanging 4 second boost with a sharp right right after it. Skip it if you have plenty of boost. If you need it, jump early so you land as you grab it.
Lake Powell helicopter	If you head straight for the ramp in the big cavern of Lake Powell, you can hit the helicopter. Sadly, there is no bonus for hitting it. You then land on a 4 second boost.
Lake Powell hidden cave tunnel	In the big cavern of Lake Powell, look left for a quay and a cave tunnel hidden near the end. The cave holds a 4 second boost and exits at the next checkpoint. It is an alternative to the ramp jump.
Lake Powell mid-air tip	While flying toward the 9 second boost in Lake Powell, try to aim at one of the 4 second boosts below you. If you miss, the 9 second boost should still carry you to the finish.
Lake Powell ramp after the archway	After an archway, a 4 second boost comes before a left-hand turn. Take the turn wide at first, then straighten up for the ramp at the end, which has a 9 second boost. It is easy to miss without good boat control.
Lake Powell start	Lake Powell starts in a very wide section of track. Stay roughly to the left, even though the first turn is to the right, then make a sharp right to a ramp with a 9 second boost.
Lake Powell waterfall cavern	In Lake Powell, right after a 9 second boost comes a small drop and a cavern. The main track goes right with a waterfall in front. Head under the middle of the waterfall to find a 4 second boost.
Lake Powell waterfall drop	Right after a checkpoint comes a left turn and a waterfall drop. Try to be on the right of the drop to land on a 4 second boost, then turn right into a tunnel.

Magnet	A magnet is an object that pulls on iron and some other metals. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole. Like poles push apart, and opposite poles pull together.
Magnetic field	A magnetic field is the area around a magnet where its force can be felt. It is often drawn as lines running from the north pole to the south pole. Iron filings can show its shape.
Magnetic Fields	At the press of a button, Neo can make a red or blue magnetic field. Each color matches the button of the same color on the Dreamcast controller. These fields work on platforms, contraptions and enemies.
Magnetic levitation	Magnetic levitation is a method of lifting an object using only magnetic forces. The magnets push against gravity so the object floats without touching anything. It is used in maglev trains and in some lab experiments.
Magnetism	Magnetism is a force caused by moving electric charges. It lets magnets pull or push on each other and on metals like iron. Magnetism and electricity are closely linked.
Magnetosphere	The magnetosphere is the region around Earth controlled by its magnetic field. It shields the planet from much of the charged particles in the solar wind. When particles leak in near the poles, they can cause the auroras.

Maken X	Maken X is a first-person hack and slash game made by Atlus for the Dreamcast. Atlus published it in Japan in 1999, and Sega brought it to other countries in 2000.
Maken X creators	Producer Kouji Okada was one of the original creators of the Megami Tensei series. Kazuma Kaneko was art director and character designer. Katsura Hashino directed the game, his first time as a game director after working as a planner.
Maken X development team	Maken X was developed by Atlus R&D1, an internal Atlus studio. Most of the team came directly from the second Persona 2 game. It was the first time this team had made a game for the Dreamcast.
Maken X development troubles	Okada and Kaneko called the development period quite turbulent. The game grew much bigger than planned, more staff joined, and work became chaotic. Trial and error on the gameplay lasted much longer than intended.
Maken X endings	Maken X has several different story paths and endings. Which one you get depends on your brainjacking and the dialogue choices the Maken makes during the game.
Maken X graphics	Earlier Atlus games had some 3D elements. Maken X was the first Atlus game to use both full 3D visuals and full-motion 3D CGI cutscenes. The team found the Dreamcast more versatile and powerful than expected.
Maken X setting	Maken X is set on a near-future Earth. The game describes it as being five minutes into the future, which is the limit of precognitive vision.
Makers of Surf Rocket Racers	Two companies made Surf Rocket Racers: CRI Middleware and Crave Entertainment. Both worked on developing and publishing the game for the Dreamcast.
Maki Yuzuki	Maki Yuzuki is the artist behind both theme songs in Orange Pocket. Her songs are the opening theme, "OrangePocket", and the ending theme.
Making a gap count	Your skater must not bail for a gap to count as found. Ramps, rails, funboxes, ledges, and even walls in many levels can have gaps to find.
Making a Profit with Trains	Balance the cost of running a train against the time it takes to move cargo. The money from delivering cargo should be more than what the train costs to run.
Making ammo from gunpowder	You can make new ammunition by using different kinds of gunpowder. Besides fighting, you will also need to solve puzzles that test logic and ideas.
Making Blue Stinger	Climax Graphics made the game. Work began in September 1996 for the Sega Saturn, but Sega asked for it to become a Dreamcast game. Full production began in December 1997, and debugging ran from late January to early March 1999.
Making Chao Stronger	Chao stats can be raised from the moment they hatch by giving them Chaos Drives or small animals found in the main stages. Stronger Chao can compete in karate and racing minigames.
Making Chaos Field	Sound and art designer Daisuke Nagata said making the game was troubled. The team lacked organization and had many people involved. Money came from publisher Able Corporation and from work on other games.
Making choices	During play, the game gives you several options to pick from. The text stops until you make a choice. Your decisions push the story in a certain direction and lead to one of several endings.
Making choices in Kanon	During play, the game gives you several options to choose from. The text stops at these points and waits until you make a choice.
Making enemies surrender	Nonviolence is possible in Soldier of Fortune. A good shot can knock an enemy's weapon out of their hand. The enemy will then cower on the floor and surrender.
Making Games for PlayStation 2	Capcom designer Shinji Mikami, creator of Resident Evil and Dino Crisis, said Sony did not give developers good enough tools. He called the PlayStation 2 the hardest system he had worked on.
Making Grand Theft Auto 2	Grand Theft Auto 2 was made by DMA Design in Dundee, with Keith Hamilton as lead programmer. The team first thought about calling it Eh Stole E' Motur, but feared that name could hurt the game's appeal around the world.
Making Hang-On	To make Hang-On, Yu Suzuki rode motorcycles a lot. Once the arcade prototype was built, he rode the prototype bike for hours every day.
Making Honey	Honey was the hardest character to make because the team paid extra attention to her face to keep her cute. Extra material for the game says she has poor eyesight and wears contact lenses.
Making Illbleed	Illbleed was made in Shinjuku, Tokyo, and work took a year and a half. At its peak, 23 staff worked on it. Programmer Kazuaki Yokozawa built a new game engine to fix problems from Blue Stinger, such as the camera.
Making Nights in 3D	The team first thought of making Nights a flat 2D sprite, fearing early 3D models would not show a hand-drawn character's personality. Nights was made in 3D, with curved flying shaped alongside the flight system and the Saturn analogue controller.
Making of Blue Stinger	Producer and co-writer Shinya Nishigaki made the game as a tribute to Western action movies. Work began in 1996 with eighteen people. Robert Short designed monsters, Pete von Sholly did storyboards, and Toshihiko Sahashi wrote the music.
Making of Death Crimson 2	Work on Death Crimson 2 started in August 1998 in Japan. The team had thirteen people: three programmers, five graphic artists, two story editors, one producer, and two sound editors.
Making of Fighting Vipers 2	Sega's AM2 team started work in early 1997 and took ten months. The team visited Alcatraz for ideas for the caged stages. Motion capture was used for the opening and win and lose poses, but most animation was hand made.
Making of Ikaruga	Director Hiroshi Iuchi started work on Ikaruga in his free time while Treasure was busy with Sin and Punishment. Five Treasure staff made the game, with help from three support staff from G.rev.
Making of Mr. Driller	Mr. Driller was designed by Yasuhito Nagaoka and produced by Hideo Yoshizawa. It was first meant to be the third Dig Dug game, with the working name Dig Dug 3.
Making of Rainbow Six	Red Storm came up with the game after the company formed in 1996. It was made alongside the Rainbow Six novel with a focus on realism and strategy. Many setbacks forced the team to crunch, and Tom Clancy himself helped very little.
Making of Rez	Production began in 1999 after Space Channel 5 was finished. Many staff came from Team Andromeda, the makers of Panzer Dragoon. Pre-production lasted a year, and staff described the work as hard but rewarding.
Making of Sakura Wars 4	The game was first meant to be set in New York. After Sega stopped the Dreamcast, the team made a celebratory game to end Ogami's story instead. It took only ten months to make.
Making of Sega Rally 2	Work on Sega Rally 2 started in March 1997, led by producer Tetsuya Mizuguchi. About half the team came from Sega AM Annex, and the rest from other Sega studios. The team built their own development tools.
Making of Sentimental Graffiti	After the 1994 hit Tokimeki Memorial, NEC Interchannel teamed Tabeta Toshio and the main staff of the Graduation series with game maker Marcus. Their goal was to make a game like Tokimeki Memorial.
Making of Silver	Silver was made by the Manchester-based UK division of Infogrames. Work began in 1995, and the game was first conceived by Warren Lancashire. Producer Lee Claire led a 25-person team that included former Ocean Software staff.
Making of Sonic Adventure	Sonic Team started work in 1997, led by director Takashi Iizuka and producer Yuji Naka. Yuji Uekawa redesigned the characters for 3D, and places in Peru and Guatemala inspired the game.
Making of Sonic Shuffle	Sega worked with Hudson Soft, the makers of Mario Party, to help build the game. Its graphics use cel shading, the same style first seen in Jet Set Radio.
Making of Soul Reaver	Crystal Dynamics started making Soul Reaver in 1997. Legal problems with Silicon Knights, who made Blood Omen, and other delays meant some planned material was cut from the game.
Making of the Game	SNK began planning The King of Fighters 2000 in June 1999. Producer Takashi Nishiyama was not on the team for the first time in the series. He created the company Dimps instead. The arcade version was nearly finished by mid-2000.
Making of Vanishing Point	Vanishing Point took 18 months to make with a team of eight people at Clockwork Games. Neil Casini is the director of Clockwork Games.
Making power-ups with the crusher	Drive a vehicle to a crusher that has a conveyor belt, then get out. The crane picks up the vehicle and crushes it. Then collect any power-up from the nearby conveyor belt.
Making Rainbow Cotton	Rainbow Cotton was made mostly by Success staff new to game making, led by founder Takato Yoshinari. Composer Kenichi Hirata already knew the series. It began as a follow-up to Panorama Cotton, called Panorama Cotton 2.
Making Segagaga	Tez Okano directed and designed Segagaga. He worked on it in secret for two years. Sega first thought it was a joke, but Hitmaker president Hisao Oguchi later let development continue. Toei Animation made the opening and cutscenes.
Making Soul Fighter	A 15-person team at Toka made Soul Fighter with help from Piggyback Interactive. They built it on PC using the 3dfx Glide API, which let them move the game to the Dreamcast in under three weeks.
Making Soulcalibur	After Soul Edge, Namco studied what made that game successful before starting the sequel. The team worked closely with Namco's Tekken team, sharing ideas and research. Yotoriyama felt this helped make the greatest weapon-based fighting action game in the world.
Making Space Channel 5	Mizuguchi interviewed girls to learn what they liked in games. At one stage the game felt cool but not so fun, so he added elements inspired by Stomp. He also invited a mime artist to help his team loosen up.
Making the Dreamcast Version	Taito tried to recreate the arcade game on Dreamcast while changing its look and controls for home play. Director Hiroshi Aoki and the team talked about this work in an October 1998 interview.
Making the Game	NHL 2K took twelve months to make. The team used motion-capture performers for player movements and recorded sound effects at GM Place in Vancouver. Visual Concepts provided the crowd assets.
Making the Igor clones laugh	In the Dissection Room, open the iron curtain and use the filled green gas tank on the pipe plug. Gas comes out of the three wall vents and all the Igor clones start laughing.
Making the music	The music was made at the same time as the game. At first the sound team worked from concept art and unfinished gameplay. Fitting many styles of music onto the game disc was one of the hardest parts.
Making the Sega CD	Sega wanted to match the PC Engine CD-ROM2 System, so it worked with JVC to design the Sega CD. Fearing leaks, Sega did not consult its American branch until the project was done.
Making the sequel	A sequel to Space Channel 5 was planned early on. Tetsuya Mizuguchi found it much easier to pitch the sequel to Sega, because Sega now knew the genre and the gameplay.
Making the show	The series cost US$3.3 million to make. It has 300 characters over thirteen episodes, a lot for 3D animation then. Bathing scenes and blood in robot fights were cut.
Making Virtua Striker	Yu Suzuki suggested that Satoshi Mifune make a football game. Mifune had worked on Space Harrier, Out Run and After Burner. Hiroyuki Nakagomi joined the small team from the Daytona USA project.
Making your own cars	PC players can make their own Re-Volt cars with the Re-Volt Car Editor. It works with 3D Studio, so you can edit existing cars or build new ones from scratch.

Mall level overview	The Mall is one of two downhill levels in Tony Hawk's Pro Skater. It is a long New York mall with closed stores, plus many balconies, ledges and stairs. Riding into the water slows you down a lot.
Mall secret tape	The secret tape is at the end of the left suspended wire above the small pool. Reach the highest balcony, grind its right edge, and ollie at the end onto a wire. If you land on the right wire, transfer left.
Mall SKATE letter E	The final letter, E, is at the atrium, over water between two ramps. Ollie at the right time, because landing in the water will slow you down.
Mall SKATE letters	The SKATE letters in the Mall are spread far apart. Get them in order, because you may not have time to skate back for any letters you missed.
Mall SKATE letters A and T	The A is at the end of the left rail over a shallow body of water. The T is on a sculpture of two curved rails before the atrium. Grind the left one to get it.
Mall SKATE letters S and K	In the Mall level, the S is on a rail to the left just before the mall entrance. The K floats above some grindable planters to the right in the fountain area.
Mall tips for vert skaters	At the start of the Mall, quarter pipes along the walls help build your special meter. The parking area and the atrium also have good ramps to air off and some bonus points to grab.
Mall: 32 Step From Mezzanine	Before leaving the atrium, use a ramp to reach the mezzanine, a higher floor with a showcase of boxes on top. At the end of that floor, ollie over the stair set that leads to the exit.

Marseille gap: Up!! Up!!	Worth 500 points. This is the same as the Up! gap, where you air up a narrow quarter pipe with a green arrow, but higher. Get plenty of speed and use a Boneless for extra height.

Marvel vs. Capcom battle format	In Marvel vs. Capcom, each battle is a single round match with two fighters on each team. Only one fighter from each team is on screen at a time, and the player may switch between them freely.

Marvel vs. Capcom: Air Attacks	To attack from the air, jump straight up or jump diagonally. Then press any single attack button while your character is in mid-air.
Marvel vs. Capcom: Air-Blocking	You can block in mid-air by holding back while jumping, as long as you are not attacking. You cannot air-block while falling or while using some characters' flying ability. Characters with Hyper Armor cannot block.
Marvel vs. Capcom: Basic Attacks	You can attack standing, crouching, or in the air. Press any single attack button to attack standing. Hold the joystick down, including either down diagonal, and press an attack button to attack crouching.
Marvel vs. Capcom: Clash of Super Heroes	Marvel vs. Capcom: Clash of Super Heroes is a fighting game that first came out in arcades. It was later brought to home systems, with versions for the Dreamcast and the PlayStation.
Marvel vs. Capcom: Crouching Block	Press the joystick diagonally down and back to block while crouching. This blocks low and middle attacks, and high attacks usually go over your head. A crouching block does not stop air attacks.
Marvel vs. Capcom: Standing Block	Push back on the joystick when the opponent attacks to block. A standing block stops middle, high, and air attacks, but not low attacks. If the opponent is not attacking, pressing back just moves you away.
Marvel vs. Capcom: Winning a Round	To win a round in Marvel vs. Capcom, you use your character's attack moves to damage the opponent. You must also block or dodge the opponent's attacks.

Master System	The Master System is the Sega Mark III renamed for release around the world. It came out in the United States in 1986. Sega hoped to follow Nintendo's worldwide success with it.
Master System accessories	Accessories for the Master System include a light gun and 3D glasses. These work with games made specially for them.
Master System Advertising	Sega said the Master System was the first console where the graphics on the box matched the graphics of the game. Its ads pushed the arcade experience. Its marketing department had only two people, which hurt its advertising.
Master System and Tonka	In 1987, Sega sold the US distribution rights for the Master System to the toy company Tonka. Tonka had no experience with electronic entertainment systems. The deal was announced shortly after the 1987 Summer CES.
Master System design	The Master System got a futuristic look meant to appeal to Western tastes. In North America, its box was white to stand apart from the black NES box, with a white grid design inspired by Apple products.
Master System games in the U.S.	Nintendo of America made a licensing plan that kept game makers working only on the NES, which limited Sega's games. Also, Sega's U.S. distributor, the toy company Tonka, chose not to bring over several Japanese Sega games.
Master System II	The Master System II is a cheaper model released in 1990 in North America, Australasia, and Europe. It has no card slot, so it only plays cartridges, and it does not work with the 3D glasses.
Master System in Japan	On October 18, 1987, the Mark III was re-released in Japan as the Master System. It cost 16,800 yen. Neither the Mark III nor the Master System seriously challenged Nintendo in Japan.
Master System launch dates	The Master System came out in North America in September 1986 and in Europe in August 1987. It reached South Korea in April 1989 and Brazil in September 1989.
Master System launch in Europe	The Master System came out in Europe in August 1987. Mastertronic sold it in the United Kingdom, Master Games in France, and Ariolasoft in West Germany. Mastertronic launched it at 99 pounds and called it an arcade in the home.
Master System Launch Package	The first North American Master System package came with the Power Base console, a light gun, and two controllers. It also included a multicart with two games, Hang-On and Safari Hunt.
Master System name	Sega of America renamed the Mark III as the Master System for Western release. Staff picked the name by throwing darts at a whiteboard of ideas. Plans for a cheaper Base System also shaped the choice.
Master System North American Reveal	The Master System was first shown in North America at the Summer Consumer Electronics Show in Chicago in June 1986. It went on sale there in September 1986 for $200.
Master System rentals	In 1989, Virgin Mastertronic began renting out the Master System console along with 20 games.
Master System Third-Party Publishers	In North America the Master System had a limited game library. Because of Nintendo's licensing practices, Sega had only two third-party American publishers, Activision and Parker Brothers. Its deals with both companies ended in 1989.
Master System UK delivery problems	Stores in the United Kingdom placed many advance orders, but Sega could not deliver stock until Boxing Day, December 26. Many stores cancelled their orders. This put Mastertronic and Master Games into money trouble.
Master System versus home computers	In Europe, Virgin Mastertronic presented the Master System as a better choice for games than the Commodore 64 and ZX Spectrum computers. This marketing helped bring European game makers to the system.

Mega Drive design	The Mega Drive was made to look more mature and less like a toy than the Famicom, to appeal to older gamers. The words 16-bit were printed on the case to show off this feature.

Mega Drive in India	In April 1994, Sega made a distribution deal with Shaw Wallace in India to get around an 80 percent import tax. Each Mega Drive unit sold there for 18,000 rupees.
Mega Drive in Japan	The Mega Drive was never popular in Japan, where the PC Engine was the rival system. In late 1995, Sega Enterprises stopped making the Mega Drive in Japan to focus on the new Sega Saturn.
Mega Drive Japan launch	Gaming magazines like Famitsu liked the Mega Drive when it came out in Japan. But it was overshadowed by Super Mario Bros. 3 for the Famicom, which came out one week before.
Mega Drive Look	A team led by Mitsushige Shiraiwa designed the Mega Drive look, drawing ideas from audiophile equipment and cars. This more mature look was meant to appeal to all ages, not just children.

Microchip	A microchip is a tiny piece of material, usually silicon, that holds many electronic circuits. Chips can contain millions of tiny switches called transistors. Microchips power computers, phones, and many household machines.
Microcode in older designs	Older CPU families used microcode so low-end models could run instructions they did not build in hardware. For example, a long multiply might be done in hardware on high-end models but as a series of additions on low-end ones.

Mode Z rising rows	In Mode Z, Gem Pairs do not fall. Instead, whole rows of Gems rise from the bottom, like in Tetris Attack. You can press the R button to make more rows rise.
Mode Z tip: raising the stack	New Crash Gems only appear with new rows, so raising the stack faster can help. But the game ends as soon as any block reaches the top of the play field, not just the Drop Alley. Do not raise it too much.

N.Y. Disaster parking lot short cut	After the first checkpoint, the track enters a multistory parking lot. On the left are checkered flag-like patterns. Head between them to cut a fair chunk off the start of the track.
N.Y. Disaster S-bend	After leaving the short cut, the track heads left. Do not take this left too sharply, since the track quickly turns right. With a little practice you can make it a convenient S-bend.
N.Y. Disaster second checkpoint choice	Past the second checkpoint, go left for a 9 second boost or straight for a ramp and a 4 second boost. Both paths join again before a tight stretch, a 4 second boost and a huge dip.
N.Y. Disaster sewage crocodile	After the tunnel comes a right turn where a huge sewage crocodile swims in the water. Take this turn wide and line up for the high boost after a dip. Jump from the top of the dip, or drop and jump back up.
N.Y. Disaster short cut exit boost	The short cut exit has a 9 second boost hanging close to the ceiling of an archway. Jump early to collect it as you land, or jump late to take off just before it, or you may hit the archway.
N.Y. Disaster: Archway Boost	After the fourth checkpoint the track turns left under a large archway. Hug the left side, because the wall almost disappears and reveals a 4 second boost before the track heads right into a subway tunnel.
N.Y. Disaster: Finish Line	Follow a long left-hand turn to the end of the tunnel. On exiting, the finish line is off to the left, with a ramp and a 4 second boost before it. Collect the boost and boost to the line.
N.Y. Disaster: Fourth Checkpoint Jump	Jump from the top of the dip and reach max speed, then cut the boost to fly a long straight. Too much boost here makes you smash into the rock at the end and miss the smooth right through the fourth checkpoint.
N.Y. Disaster: Subway Platform Boost	The subway tunnel takes a split, but either way leads to the subway platform with a 9 second boost on it. Jump at the boost and slide to the other side. The split then joins again for another checkpoint.
N.Y. Disaster: Subway Train Dip	After a long right-hand turn you see a subway train. Just before it is a dip where you should keep left. Do not hug the wall too much, or you will miss the 4 second boost at the bottom.
