Nile Adventure	Nile Adventure is a bonus track in Hydro Thunder. It is the only bonus track that is not a circuit course. It is also the longest track of all, more than a third longer than most others based on time.
Nile Adventure Canal Jump	After the archways comes a long upward stretch that throws you high into the air over a long, thin canal. It ends in a long, narrow slope with a 4 second boost on the way down.
Nile Adventure Checkpoint Three	Take the right hand turn after the straight to find checkpoint three under an archway. The track then goes right, then left, onto a long stretch where you can see the tunnel exit.
Nile Adventure drop boost	After the first checkpoint, a long straight has a drop with a 4 second boost in the air. Jump before the drop and boost to it, or drop and jump right away to grab it.
Nile Adventure Falling Sarcophagi	Sarcophagi drop down as you race through the tunnel. On the short straight they may hit you as you jump for a hanging 9 second boost. Try to grab it as you land, since a sharp right turn follows.
Nile Adventure Guardian Drop	Just before a guardian statue in Nile Adventure is a 4 second boost and a long drop. If you are jumping along the straight, land before the drop. The second check point is at the bottom.
Nile Adventure Hidden Sarcophagus Path	At the end of the straight, a sarcophagus opens to show a hidden section of track. It holds two 9 second boosts, one hidden at the entrance, but it is actually a longer way through.
Nile Adventure Sarcophagus Tunnel	The tunnel on Nile Adventure is called the nastiest part of the track. It is lined with sarcophagi, and triangular forms on both sides of the track slow you down if you hit them, which is easy to do.
Nile Adventure Snake Tunnel	A wide tunnel with a snake's head at the front leads inside the snake's innards. The track turns left, then into a long right hander, with 4 second boosts along the way.
Nile Adventure Sphinx Jump	At the end of the rock tunnel, a 4 second boost sits before a large drop and a sphinx's head guarding another tunnel. Jump before the drop to fly through the sphinx's face and into the tunnel.
Nile Adventure start and bridge boost	The race starts on a long straightaway heading for a bridge with three archways. Head for the middle archway and try to boost over it to get a hidden 4 second boost.
Nile Adventure Three Archways Shortcut	After the second check point, skip the two tunnel entrances and look up for three archways split by two pillars. Land at the entrance between the pillars to get a 9 second boost and instant maximum speed.
Nile Adventure Tunnel Boosts	Inside the tunnel, a sharp left after a long right holds a 4 second boost. After another long right, the next left has a second 4 second boost that leads onto a short straightaway.
Nile Adventure Tunnel Exit Stretch	On the long stretch leading to the tunnel exit, large sections of roof drop down to keep you at track level. Do not try jumping here.
Nile Adventure tunnel turns	Inside the tunnel the water slopes downward between turns. The turns go left, right, right, then left. A 4 second boost waits after the first right turn.
Nile Adventure twin ramps	Just after the track turns right under a bridge, there is a pair of ramps. The closest ramp gives a 9 second boost and the farther ramp gives a 4 second boost.
Nile Adventure waterfalls and tunnel	Past the drop are two waterfalls, one on each side, and a tunnel entrance. Take the tunnel, because the waterfalls only hide rocks.

Origin of Code: Veronica	Code: Veronica began after Capcom failed to bring Resident Evil 2 to the Sega Saturn without a big loss in quality. Producer Shinji Mikami was asked to make something new for Sega fans, so work started on an original Saturn game.
Origin of Rainbow Six	Rainbow Six began as an idea called HRT at Red Storm Entertainment, chosen from about 100 other ideas. HRT was about the FBI Hostage Rescue Team saving hostages from criminals and terrorists.
Origin of Sakura Wars	Oji Hiroi came up with the idea for Sakura Wars in 1990. He got the idea after seeing a Japanese stage show of the play Shanghai Rhapsody. He was impressed by the spectacle of the acting troop on stage.
Origin of the Ashford Twins	Alexia and Alfred Ashford were genetically created in 1971 by their father Alexander. He cloned them from the DNA of Veronica Ashford, the first leader of the Ashford clan, who was known for her superior IQ and sociopathic tendencies.
Origin of the Bangai-O idea	The idea came from Treasure worker Mitsuru Yaida, known as Yaiman. He remembered an older shooting game that amazed him with how many bullets it could show on screen at once. This led him to build a prototype.
Origin of the crazy style	Gus pioneered the crazy style of driving when he bought his 1955 Jalopy.
Origin of the Name Kitty	Hello Kitty's designer Shimizu took the name Kitty from Lewis Carroll's book Through the Looking-Glass. Early in the book, Alice plays with a cat she calls Kitty.
Origin of the Sega Name	The name Sega is short for Service Games. It was first used in 1954 on the Diamond Star Machine, which was a slot machine.
Origin of the term console war	Video game journalists called the aggressive marketing between console makers a war or battle as early as August 1988. With each new console generation, journalists and players kept using similar words, such as system wars and console wars.
Origin of the Yuke's name	The company Yuke's was named after the high school nickname of its founder, Yukinori Taniguchi.
Origin of two-digit dates	Using two-digit dates for convenience started before computers existed. It only became a problem once stored dates were used in calculations.
Origin Systems	Origin Systems is a game company based in Austin, Texas. It is known for the Ultima role-playing series and the Wing Commander space combat series. Electronic Arts bought it in the early 1990s.

Origins of Sonic Adventure	Nights into Dreams designer Takashi Iizuka felt Sonic fans had been let down because Sonic Team was not focusing on the series. Kazuyuki Hoshino, art director on Sonic Adventure, thought Sonic had become outdated during the Saturn years.

Pamphlet	The Pamphlet is a cosmetic item that holds info about items, weapons, characters, foes and bosses you learn about. Info gathered by earlier characters carries over when you switch, and it sometimes gives useful hints.
Panama Canal	The Panama Canal crosses Panama and links the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. The United States finished it in 1914. It uses locks to raise and lower ships, and Panama took full control of it in 1999.
Panasonic 3DO	The Panasonic 3DO is a game console released in 1993, based on a design by The 3DO Company. It uses CDs for games and was one of the first 32-bit home systems. Its high launch price limited sales.
Pancake	A pancake is a flat, round cake made from a batter of flour, eggs, and milk, cooked on a hot pan. Pancakes are eaten in many countries. In North America they are often served with butter and syrup.
Pancreas	The pancreas is an organ behind the stomach. It makes juices that help digest food. It also makes insulin and other hormones that control the amount of sugar in the blood.
Panda	The giant panda is a bear with black and white fur. It lives in mountain forests in China. Pandas eat mostly bamboo. Very few are left in the wild, so they are in danger.

Pandora (moon)	Pandora is a small moon of Saturn found in Voyager 1 pictures in 1980. It orbits just outside Saturn's narrow F ring. Together with Prometheus, it helps keep the ring in shape.
Pandora Project	Pandora Project is the secret group hidden behind City Hall. Its goal is to stop the moon city from invading the main world. Ikuo Fuyuki, Marufuji's boss, reveals the truth about it.

Paneer	Paneer is a fresh cheese common in India and nearby lands. It is made by curdling hot milk with lemon juice or vinegar, then pressing the curds. It does not melt easily, so it is often cooked in curries.
Panettone	Panettone is a tall, sweet bread from Milan, Italy. It is made with yeast dough, candied fruit, and raisins. It is a popular gift and treat at Christmas and New Year.
Pangolin	Pangolins are mammals covered in hard scales. They live in Africa and Asia and eat ants and termites with their long tongues. When in danger, a pangolin rolls into a tight ball.
Panic Horror	Dino Crisis was called panic horror instead of survival horror like Resident Evil. Its dinosaurs are smart and quick and can chase the player from room to room. Mikami compared it to riding a roller coaster.

Panning the camera	Hold Special 2 and press Forward, Backward or Turn Left/Right to pan the camera in GTA2. Letting go centers the view again.
Panzer Dragoon	Panzer Dragoon is a Sega shooting game first released for the Sega Saturn in 1995. The player rides a flying dragon and shoots enemies. It led to sequels such as Panzer Dragoon Zwei and Panzer Dragoon Saga.
Panzer Dragoon Saga Team	Some of the people who made Panzer Dragoon Saga went on to work at Smilebit. There they made Jet Set Radio, a game they wanted to be completely different from Panzer Dragoon.
Panzer Front	Panzer Front is a World War II tank simulation game made by Enterbrain. It came out in Japan in 1999 for the PlayStation and the Dreamcast.
Panzer Front bis	Panzer Front bis is an updated version for the PlayStation, out in Japan on February 8, 2001. It has all the original tanks and missions, plus more tanks, ten new scenarios, and a mission editor.
Paper	Paper is a thin material made from plant fibers and used for writing and printing. It was invented in China about 2,000 years ago. Its making is often credited to Cai Lun.
Paperboy	Paperboy is an arcade game made by Atari Games in the mid-1980s. The player rides a bike and throws newspapers to houses along a street. The arcade machine uses bicycle handlebars as its controller.

Paramaribo	Paramaribo is the capital and largest city of Suriname, in South America. It is a port on the Suriname River near the coast. Its old center has many Dutch colonial wooden buildings.
Parappa the Rapper	Parappa the Rapper is a rhythm game for the Sony PlayStation, first released in Japan in 1996. Players press buttons in time with music as a cartoon dog raps. It helped make music games popular.
PaRappa the Rapper influence	Ueda was inspired by a demo of the PlayStation rhythm game PaRappa the Rapper at the 1996 Tokyo Game Show. He called it the first game with pop culture like that, and decided to make a true game for adults.
Paris	Paris is the capital and largest city of France, on the Seine River. It is known for art, fashion, and food. Famous sights include the Eiffel Tower, the Louvre museum, and Notre Dame Cathedral.

Parrot	Parrots are colorful birds with curved beaks, found mostly in warm parts of the world. Many can copy human speech and other sounds. They use their strong beaks to crack nuts and seeds.

Parthenon	The Parthenon is a temple on the Acropolis in Athens, Greece, built in the 400s BC. It was made for the goddess Athena and is one of the most famous examples of ancient Greek building.
Parthian Empire	The Parthian Empire was a large empire centered in what is now Iran. It fought many wars against Rome. Parthian horse archers were famous for shooting arrows while riding away.

Passing cars at corners	It is often better to wait behind a group of cars until they get through a corner, then speed past them on the straight. Passing before or during the corner can cause damage or a crash.

Pasta	Pasta is a food made from wheat flour and water, sometimes with eggs. It comes in many shapes, such as spaghetti and macaroni. It is boiled and served with sauces and is a main food in Italy.

Pavlova	Pavlova is a dessert with a crisp meringue shell and a soft inside. It is topped with whipped cream and fresh fruit. Australia and New Zealand both claim to have invented it, and it was named after a Russian ballerina.

PC-98	The PC-98 is a series of personal computers made by NEC in Japan. It uses Intel processors but is not fully IBM PC compatible. For many years it was the leading computer in Japan.
PC-FX Games	The PC-FX has no polygon processor, so it does not draw 3D shapes the way some other systems do. NEC sold it as a system for 2D games and full motion video games.
PCX1 and Apocalypse 3D	The single-chip PCX1 was sold in stores as the VideoLogic Apocalypse 3D. It had an improved design with more texture memory, so it ran more games than the older Midas3.
PCX2	The PCX2 is a refined PCX1 that runs 6 MHz faster. More of the work is done on the chip instead of the driver, and it adds bilinear filtering. It is sold on the Matrox M3D and Videologic Apocalypse 3Dx cards.
Peacock	The peacock is the male peafowl, known for its long, colorful tail feathers with eye-like spots. It spreads its tail in a fan to attract females. Peafowl come from South Asia.

Peking duck	Peking duck is a famous roast duck dish from Beijing, China. The duck is prized for its thin, crisp skin. It is often served sliced with thin pancakes, sweet sauce, and green onions.
Pelican	Pelicans are large water birds with long bills and a stretchy pouch of skin under the bill. They use the pouch to scoop up fish. Some kinds dive from the air to catch food.
Pelmeni	Pelmeni are small dumplings from Russia, often linked to Siberia. Thin dough is wrapped around a filling of minced meat, usually pork, beef, or lamb. They are boiled and often served with butter or sour cream.
Pelota	Pelota is a family of court games from the Basque region of Spain and France. Players hit a ball against a wall using the hand, a bat, a racket, or a basket. Jai alai is one well known form.
Pen Pen	The Pen Pen are an alien race from Iced Planet. They were named Pen Pen because the closest animal on Earth they look like is the penguin. They may have their own language, but humans cannot understand it.

Penelope Pitstop	Penelope Pitstop is a character in the game. She is voiced by Janet Waldo, who plays her role again.
Penguin	Penguins are birds that cannot fly but are excellent swimmers. Most live in the Southern Hemisphere, many in cold places like Antarctica. The emperor penguin is the largest kind.
Penicillin	Penicillin is an antibiotic made from a mold. It was discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928 and became widely used in the 1940s. It kills many kinds of bacteria and has saved millions of lives.
Peninsula	A peninsula is land with water on three sides. It stays joined to a larger piece of land. Florida and Italy are well-known peninsulas.
Pentium 4 patch	The first version of the game had performance problems on computers with Pentium 4 processors. A patch was released to fix these problems.
Pentium II	The Pentium II is a computer processor made by Intel, introduced in 1997. It came in a cartridge that plugs into a slot rather than a socket. It added MMX instructions for faster multimedia.
Pepper Ann	Pepper Ann is an American Disney cartoon series that began in 1997. It follows a lively 12-year-old girl dealing with life in middle school.
Perception System	NFL 2K uses what Sega's Greg Thomas called a perception system. Each player on the field reacts on his own to what is happening around him during a play.
Percival Lowell	Percival Lowell was an American businessman and astronomer who founded Lowell Observatory in Flagstaff, Arizona. He believed he saw canals on Mars built by living beings. He also searched for an unknown planet beyond Neptune, which led to Pluto's discovery.
Peregrine Falcon	The peregrine falcon is a bird of prey found on every continent except Antarctica. It is the fastest animal known, diving at well over 300 kilometers per hour to catch other birds. Some now nest on tall city buildings.
Perfect Chaos	Chaos absorbs the Chaos Emeralds and transforms into Perfect Chaos. It turns against Robotnik and destroys Station Square. Sonic uses the Chaos Emeralds to become Super Sonic and defeats it.

Perfect Ratings in Story Mode	Each Report in the Single Player Story Mode of Space Channel 5: Part 2 can get a perfect rating. A top goal for skilled players is to earn a perfect rating on every Report.
Perfect round	In Garou: Mark of the Wolves, a perfect round means winning a round without taking any damage.
Performance Mega Memory Card	The Performance Mega Memory Card works like a 4X Memory Card. You pick the memory card page with a switch on its back. You must take it out of the controller before you can change the page.
Performance Memory Card	The Performance Memory Card is a basic memory card for the Dreamcast made by another company, not Sega. It has 200 blocks of storage, the same as a VMU.
Periscope	Periscope was a submarine simulator and the first arcade electro-mechanical game Sega made, released in the late 1960s. It had new light and sound effects and was a hit in Japan. It helped set the 25-cent price per play in US arcades.
Periscope and Missile	Periscope was the first arcade game made by Sega. It was an electromechanical game. Sega followed it with Missile in 1969.
Periscope in the United States	In the US, Periscope was placed in malls and department stores. It became the first arcade game in the US to cost 25 cents per play. After its success, Sega made eight to ten games per year for two years.
Persepolis	Persepolis was a grand capital of the ancient Persian Empire, in what is now Iran. It was begun by King Darius the Great and is known for its stone columns and carvings. Alexander the Great burned it.
Persian Empire	The Persian Empire was founded by Cyrus the Great in what is now Iran. At its height it stretched from Egypt to India. It was known for good roads, a royal mail system, and allowing many peoples to keep their customs.
Persona	Persona is one of the flagship game series from Atlus, along with Megami Tensei. It is a Japanese role-playing game series.
Personal Action	Personal action is a taunt unique to each character. If it is completed successfully, it gives an extra benefit. For example, Ryu's personal action lowers his stun gauge.
Personal Aquarium	Once you catch a fish, you can put it into your personal aquarium. There you can feed the fish and raise it.
Personal computer	A personal computer is a computer made for one person to use at home or work. Small, affordable models became popular in the late 1970s and 1980s. Today they are used for writing, games, and the Internet.
Personal Fouls	NBA Showtime adds personal fouls. Each shove on another player counts as a foul. After a certain number of fouls, the other team gets a free throw.
Personification	Personification is giving human traits to animals, objects, or ideas. Saying "the wind whispered" or "the sun smiled" are examples. Poets and storytellers use it to make writing more vivid.
Peru	Peru is a country on the west coast of South America with its capital in Lima. It was the center of the Inca Empire. The ancient Inca city of Machu Picchu sits high in its Andes Mountains.
Pet Death	A pet can die from poor care, sickness, old age, or in a few versions, predators. Japanese toys show a ghost and headstone, while English versions show an angel. If an old pet dies with no offspring, the family line ends.
Petanque	Petanque is a French ball game in which players stand in a small circle and toss metal balls toward a small wooden ball. The aim is to land closest to it. It began in southern France in the early 1900s.
Pete Conrad	Pete Conrad commanded Apollo 12 in 1969 and became the third person to walk on the Moon. He also flew on Gemini 5 and Gemini 11. He later commanded the first crew to live aboard Skylab.
Petit-Ange	Petit-Ange is Tsubame's Pata-Pi. Its name is French for Little Angel, and it is basically dumb. It transforms into the Diva Erinyes.
Petra	Petra is an ancient city in what is now Jordan. Its buildings were carved straight into pink and red rock cliffs. It was the capital of the Nabataeans and was a major stop on trade routes.
Petrichor	Petrichor is the pleasant, earthy smell that often comes with the first rain after a dry spell. The word was coined by two Australian scientists in the 1960s. The smell comes partly from oils and compounds released from soil and rocks.
Phantasy Star	Phantasy Star is a 1987 game for the Master System. Yuji Naka made pseudo-3D animation effects for it. He met artist Naoto Ohshima while working on this game.
Phantasy Star II	Phantasy Star II is a role-playing game made by Sega for the Mega Drive, or Genesis, first released in 1989. It is set about a thousand years after the first game. Its hero, Rolf, lives on the planet Motavia.

Phantasy Star III: Generations of Doom	Phantasy Star III is a role-playing game for the Sega Genesis. The story spans three generations of heroes. Choices about whom the hero marries change who leads the next generation.
Phantasy Star IV	Phantasy Star IV: The End of the Millennium is a role-playing game made by Sega for the Mega Drive, or Genesis. Its hero is a young hunter named Chaz. The game ties together the story of the earlier games.
Phantasy Star IV: The End of the Millennium	Phantasy Star IV is a role-playing game for the Sega Genesis. It ends the story of the original Phantasy Star series. It tells its story with comic-book style picture panels.
Phantasy Star Online	Phantasy Star Online is an online role-playing game for the Dreamcast, made by Sonic Team and published by Sega in 2000. Players team up over the internet to complete quests, collect items and fight enemies.
Phantasy Star Online 4x Memory Card	A limited edition Phantasy Star Online 4x Memory Card came out in Japan with the game. It was blue and had the Phantasy Star Online logo printed on the case.
Phantasy Star Online and Earlier Games	Phantasy Star Online does not continue the story of the earlier Phantasy Star games. The team was free to break from the older games. Yuji Naka said he felt freed by this choice.
Phantasy Star Online Art Style	Few Phantasy Star IV staff still worked at Sega, so the art team did not copy the old style. They kept only the science fiction look and some enemy and item names.
Phantasy Star Online Battle Music	The music is built from short four-bar melodies that change with the action. When an enemy shows up, the game plays music that goes with that enemy.
Phantasy Star Online beta test	In Japan, Sonic Team gave beta versions of Phantasy Star Online to 10,000 people who pre-ordered the game. This helped find problems with many kinds of equipment and internet services. 90% of the testers were able to play online.
Phantasy Star Online Episode I & II	This fact book has no record of a game by this name. The known Dreamcast game is Phantasy Star Online, an online role-playing game by Sonic Team.
Phantasy Star Online inspirations	Yuji Naka studied three popular western online RPGs: Diablo, Ultima Online, and EverQuest. Diablo impressed him most because its graphics and action were so smooth. Sonic Team made Diablo their main inspiration and set out to outclass it.
Phantasy Star Online Music	Hideaki Kobayashi made the music using a Roland JV-2080 synthesizer. Some tracks, including the theme song, use a live orchestra. Calm scenes have soft ambient music, while battles have more rhythm and melody.
Phantasy Star Online network	Sonic Team based the online system for Phantasy Star Online on the one from ChuChu Rocket!. The new network had to connect players in different countries, so the team tested many internet providers, dial-up modems and cable modems.
Phantasy Star Online story	Thousands of refugees flee their dying home planet aboard the spaceship Pioneer 2 and arrive at planet Ragol. As they contact colonists sent ahead on Pioneer 1, a huge explosion shakes the planet. The story is unrelated to the original Phantasy Star series.

Phantasy Star Online Version 2	Phantasy Star Online Version 2 is an updated version of Sega's online role-playing game for the Dreamcast. It adds a higher difficulty level, a higher level limit, and new modes.
Phantasy Star series	Phantasy Star Online is a sub-series of Sega's Phantasy Star games. The Phantasy Star series began in 1987.
Pharoah Illusion	Pharoah Illusion is Anakaris's only unique Hyper Combo in MvC2. He becomes a giant and bats the opponent between his hands. It starts instantly, and you press punch and kick in rhythm to keep juggling.

Philadelphia custom items	The Philadelphia map marks gray liberty bells. It also shows an aqua valve, which you use to drain the fountain.
Philately	Philately is the collecting and study of postage stamps. Collectors look at a stamp's design, printing, and history, and some rare stamps are worth large sums. The hobby began soon after Britain issued the first postage stamp in 1840.
Philippines	The Philippines is a country in Southeast Asia made of more than 7,000 islands, with its capital in Manila. It was ruled by Spain and then the United States. It became independent in 1946.
Philips CD-i	The CD-i format was announced in the late 1980s, and the first machines came out in 1991. Its main selling point was that it was more than a game machine and could be used for multimedia. It was discontinued in 1998.

Phnom Penh	Phnom Penh is the capital of Cambodia, where the Mekong and Tonle Sap rivers meet. The Khmer Rouge forced people out of the city in 1975. It has slowly grown again since then.
Pho	Pho is a Vietnamese soup made with broth, rice noodles, and herbs. It is usually served with thin slices of beef or chicken. Diners often add lime, bean sprouts, and chili.
Phobos	Phobos is the larger and closer of the two moons of Mars. It is small, dark, and shaped like a lumpy potato, with a very large crater called Stickney. It circles Mars faster than Mars turns.
Phobos (moon)	Phobos is the larger of the two moons of Mars. It is small, dark, and shaped like a lumpy potato. It orbits very close to Mars and slowly spirals inward.
Phoebe (moon)	Phoebe is a distant moon of Saturn, discovered in 1899. It was the first moon found using photographs. It is dark and orbits backward, so it may be a captured object.
Phoenicia	Phoenicia was an ancient land of sea traders on the coast of what is now Lebanon. Its main cities included Tyre and Sidon. The Phoenicians made an alphabet that later led to the Greek and Latin alphabets.
Phoenicians	The Phoenicians were sailors and traders from the coast of what is now Lebanon. They set up trading cities around the Mediterranean, including Carthage. Their alphabet became the basis for the Greek and Latin alphabets.
Phoenix and Dragon Mirrors	The phoenix mirror and the dragon mirror are a pair of mirrors at the heart of Ryo's story. Shenhua's family is closely tied to these two mirrors.

Phone line busy during dial-up	Dial-up uses the normal telephone network. Because of this, you cannot use your phone line for talking until the Internet call is finished.
Phone line use	Broadband does not need a phone line all to itself. You can be online and still make and receive voice calls without a second phone line.
Phonograph	The phonograph was invented by Thomas Edison in 1877. It recorded sound as grooves on a cylinder, at first wrapped in tinfoil, and could play the sound back. It was the first practical machine for recording and playing back sound.
Phosphorescence	Phosphorescence is a glow that some materials give off after they absorb light. Unlike fluorescence, the glow keeps going for a while after the light source is removed. Glow-in-the-dark toys and watch dials use this effect.
Photo exhibition goal	Kouhei must find his own model for the photo exhibition at the coming school festival. He turns to one of the girls, now emotionally scarred, and hopes to convince her to be his model.
Photoelectric effect	The photoelectric effect happens when light hits a metal and knocks electrons loose. Albert Einstein explained it by saying light comes in small packets of energy. This effect is used in solar cells and light sensors.
Photography	Photography is the art of making pictures by capturing light, usually on film. Cameras use a lens to focus light, and the film is later developed into prints. New digital cameras store pictures as computer files instead.
Photosynthesis	Photosynthesis is the way green plants make their own food. Using sunlight, they turn water and carbon dioxide into sugar and give off oxygen. A green substance called chlorophyll helps plants capture the light.

PlayStation 2	Sony officially announced the PlayStation 2 on March 2, 1999. Sony wanted it to be a gateway for all types of home entertainment and to one day replace the desktop computer in the home.

PowerVR	PowerVR is a division of Imagination Technologies, formerly called VideoLogic. It develops hardware and software for 2D and 3D rendering and for video encoding and decoding.
PowerVR depth speed	The PowerVR hardware typically works out the depths for each polygon for one tile row in just 1 cycle.
PowerVR for laptops	As the 3D market changed quickly, PowerVR brought out new versions with low-power electronics aimed at laptop computers. These grew into designs that could fit into system-on-a-chip parts for handheld devices.
PowerVR licensing	PowerVR does not make its own chips. Instead it licenses its chip designs and patents to other companies, such as NEC, Texas Instruments, Intel, Sony, and STMicroelectronics.
PowerVR MBX and MBX Lite	PowerVR MBX is a low power graphics design that comes in two versions, MBX and MBX Lite. Both have the same features, but MBX is tuned for speed and MBX Lite is tuned for low power use.
PowerVR on-chip memory	Because PowerVR renders one tile at a time, the whole tile can sit in fast on-chip memory. It is then flushed to video memory before the next tile, and each tile is normally visited once per frame.
PowerVR origins	PowerVR was first made to compete in the desktop PC market for 3D hardware accelerators. Its goal was a better price-performance ratio than existing products, such as those from 3dfx Interactive.
PowerVR tiles	PowerVR splits the display into rectangular sections in a grid pattern. Each section is called a tile. Each tile has a list of the triangles that visibly overlap it, and each tile is rendered in turn to make the final image.
PowerVR vs Voodoo	PowerVR PCX cards are budget products that run current games well. They lack some features of 3DFX Voodoo cards, such as certain blending modes. All models support DirectX 3.0 and PowerSGL, and some games have MiniGL drivers.
PowerVR2 (CLX2)	The PowerVR2, also called PowerVR Series2, is the second generation PowerVR chip. Its chip codename is CLX2. It is the graphics chip inside the Sega Dreamcast console.
PowerVR3 KYRO	The PowerVR3 STG4000 KYRO is the third generation PowerVR chip, released in 2000. It is made by new partner STMicroelectronics. Its design was reworked for better game compatibility and uses two pipelines for more speed.

Prince of Persia 3D development	Prince of Persia 3D began active development in 1997 at Mindscape. Preproduction started in April 1996, when the first proposals were made. Around 20 people worked on the game, plus a few contractors in Canada who helped with cutscenes.
Prince of Persia 3D game engine	Prince of Persia 3D uses the NetImmerse game engine, which handles polygon models and particle effects. Character animation and AI behaviour are handled by Motion Factory's Motivate system. The in-house team programmed the other actions and elements.
Prince of Persia 3D graphics	The engine lets the game have both indoor and outdoor areas without many limits. Polygon models can warp, so you can see things like the Prince breathing. A 3D accelerator is required to play.
Prince of Persia 3D music	The music for Prince of Persia 3D was written by three composers working together: Tom Rettig, Jonelle Adkisson and Greg Rahn.
Prince of Persia 3D PlayStation version	A PlayStation version based on the PC game was being made, with gameplay changes for action game fans. It was cancelled so the staff could focus on the Dreamcast version.
Prince of Persia 3D publisher	Prince of Persia 3D was published under the Red Orb Entertainment brand. Red Orb was split away from Broderbund during the buyout and continued to support Mindscape.
Prince of Persia 3D release	Broderbund announced the game in April 1998 and showed it at E3 that year. It came out for Windows in North America on September 17, 1999, and in Europe on October 1. Patches fixing bugs followed in the next weeks.
Prince of Persia 3D Setting	The environments, architecture, and enemies in Prince of Persia 3D draw on the history and religion of Medieval Persia. Much of the architecture is based on Persia during the 9th and 12th century.
Prince of Persia 3D story	The Sultan travels with the newly married Prince and Princess to visit his brother Assan, whose kingdom lies south of Persia. During an entertainment, Assan's guards kill the Sultan's guard and imprison the Prince.
Prince of Persia 3D story and dialogue	The scenario for Prince of Persia 3D was co-written by series creator Jordan Mechner. The dialogue in the cutscenes was written by John Morgan.
Prince of Persia 3D Story Style	The storyline of Prince of Persia 3D was meant to copy the style of One Thousand and One Nights. The team put a lot of effort into the story and the design of the places in the game.
Prince of Persia 3D Sword Fighting	The battles in Prince of Persia 3D take ideas from earlier Prince of Persia games and from Bushido Blade. Two fighting experts, one a movie weapon props worker and one an ex-Marine, were filmed doing moves that were copied in the game.

Re-Volt car handling for newcomers	Most cars in Re-Volt are nimble and fast, so many newcomers find them hard to control. The Junior RC difficulty slows the pace of the game to help new players.
Re-Volt car stats	Each car has Speed, Acceleration, Weight, and Transmission stats. Speed is top speed, which the Turbo Battery Power-Up can raise for a short time. Weight, in kilograms, affects acceleration, grip, and resistance to Pick Ups.
Re-Volt car transmission	Transmission tells you how a car is driven in Re-Volt. A car can be four wheel drive, front wheel drive, or rear wheel drive. It is one of the stats that shape how the car handles.
Re-Volt cars	Re-Volt has thirty one different kinds of cars. Each car has an official name that is shown in the Car Selection section.
Re-Volt Championship mode	Championship is a competitive mode in Re-Volt. You must place 3rd or higher to keep competing, and you must win to unlock new cars and tracks.
Re-Volt Championship points	In Re-Volt, finishing a race in first, second, or third place scores you points. These points move you to a higher position in Championship mode.
Re-Volt cheat codes	Re-Volt has cheat codes that can help you win races faster. You turn them on by typing their words on the Name Wheel before you pick your car and track.
Re-Volt Console difficulty	Console is the Medium difficulty in Re-Volt. Cars travel at full speed and collisions with other cars are simple. Hitting walls only makes you lose speed, not control, so it is forgiving for new players.
Re-Volt direction arrow and wrong way X	In Re-Volt, an arrow sometimes appears to show which way to go so you do not get lost. A blinking letter X means you are going the wrong way. The arrow shows at the bottom left or top middle, depending on game version.
Re-Volt goal	In Re-Volt, your goal is to complete a number of laps and finish in the top 3. Every race you win lets you unlock new cars and tracks to use.

Re-Volt learning curve	Re-Volt can take time to learn. New players may find it hard at first, so practice on the courses to get better.

Resident Evil 2 Outskirts: Dumpster Alley	After the second staircase, grab the hidden Handgun Bullets in the trash pile to the right. Then climb onto the dumpster, jump down the other side, and run along the right-hand wall to the gate at the end.
Resident Evil 2 Outskirts: Female Zombie by the Dumpster	If the female zombie across from the dumpster notices you, shoot her from where you stand until she falls. Then quickly cross the dumpster. Stay close to the right-hand wall to avoid being grabbed.
Resident Evil 2 Outskirts: Inside the Bus	Take the box of Handgun Bullets on top of the bag. Aim down and shoot the female zombie on the ground until she is dead. Kill the next zombie, or run past him after he falls once, and exit the far doors.
Resident Evil 2 Outskirts: Street to the Police Station	Do not shoot the zombies on this street, since you can easily run past them. Run diagonally past the first two, then along the police cars to the gate at the end, which leads to the police station grounds.
Resident Evil 2 Outskirts: Zombie Crowd Near the Bus	A large group of zombies waits outside the bus. Run forward without stopping and go through the bus doors to reach safety. If you stop, the zombies may overrun you and throw you back and forth until you die.

Rez and Wassily Kandinsky	Mizuguchi felt his experience in Zurich was like the inspiration of Wassily Kandinsky, a Russian painter. Kandinsky was said to paint a canvas of the sounds that he saw. Mizuguchi tied this idea of mixing sight and sound to Rez.

Sakura Wars	Sakura Wars is the first game in the Sakura Wars series. It came out in 1996 for the Sega Saturn. It was also brought to other systems, including the Dreamcast and Windows PCs.
Sakura Wars (the game)	Sakura Wars is a cross-genre game made by Sega and Red Company and published by Sega in 1996 for the Sega Saturn. Sega calls it a dramatic adventure game. It mixes tactical role-playing, dating sim, and visual novel play.
Sakura Wars 2	Sakura Wars 2: Thou Shalt Not Die is the direct sequel to Sakura Wars. It came out in 1998.
Sakura Wars 2 animated cutscenes	Production I.G made the animated cutscenes, and Shinji Takagi directed them. This was the studio's first Sakura Wars work. Hiroi chose them after seeing their film Ghost in the Shell.
Sakura Wars 2 battles	Sakura Wars 2 keeps turn-based grid battles but raises the action list to six and adds cinematic attacks. The leader can also order the whole squad into specific battle formations.
Sakura Wars 2 development staff	Series creator Oji Hiroi was general producer and Tomoyuki Ito was chief director. Satoru Akahori wrote the story. Hidenori Matsubara and Kosuke Fujishima designed the characters, and Takaharu Terada was battle designer.
Sakura Wars 2 music	Kohei Tanaka was the only composer and the musical director. Most songs use the Saturn's sound chip, with some live tracks. Tanaka wanted the synthesized music to sound as close to live music as he could.
Sakura Wars 2 story	The main story is darker than the first game. It has political parts and more sad events for the main cast. Kyogoku's attempted coup is based on the February 26 Incident.
Sakura Wars 2 subtitle	The subtitle Thou Shalt Not Die comes from a famous anti-war poem by Japanese author and poet Akiko Yosano. It ties into the game's themes and story.
Sakura Wars 2 voice cast	The main cast from the first Sakura Wars game came back to voice their roles in Sakura Wars 2. Two new cast members joined: Maya Okamoto as Orihime and Kazue Ikura as Reni.
Sakura Wars 2: Thou Shalt Not Die	Sakura Wars 2: Thou Shalt Not Die is the sequel to the first Sakura Wars. It came out for the Sega Saturn in 1998 and was the last game made for that system. It was also brought to the Dreamcast and Windows.
Sakura Wars 3 cutscenes	Making the cutscenes took a lot of work, needing 200 different cuts and 4000 sheets of character movements. The storyboards were as big as a half-hour original video animation. The anime parts were directed by Shinji Takagi and made by Production I.G.
Sakura Wars 3 developers	Sakura Wars 3 was made by Red Company and Overworks, a division of Sega. Overworks was one of nine semi-independent Sega studios formed when Sega reorganized its arcade and console teams in 2000.
Sakura Wars 3 on Dreamcast	The first two games were on the Sega Saturn, but Sakura Wars 3 was made for the Dreamcast. Because it was a new system, the team rebuilt the game engine and systems from scratch to use the Dreamcast's features.
Sakura Wars 3 origins	Concept work for Sakura Wars 3 began while Sakura Wars 2: Thou Shalt Not Die was still being made. The ending of the second game leads directly into the events of Sakura Wars 3.
Sakura Wars 3 Paris research	To show Paris in the 1920s properly, Hiroi and other staff traveled to Paris to study its culture and setting. They talked with French natives who could speak Japanese and made copies of adverts from the 1920s.
Sakura Wars 3 setting	The idea of moving the setting from Tokyo to Paris came from Akahori. Talking with people is a major theme of the game. The story drew from the short story The Dancing Girl by Mori Ogai.
Sakura Wars 3 staff	Series creator Oji Hiroi was general producer, with director Akira Nishino and writer Satoru Akahori. Hidenori Matsubara and Kosuke Fujishima designed the new characters, and Mika Akitaka designed the mecha. Noriyoshi Ohba was executive producer.
Sakura Wars 3 Story	In 1926, Imperial Japanese Navy Lieutenant Ichiro Ogami arrives in Paris. He must train a new team set up by the government to fight supernatural threats. The team is called the Paris Combat Revue.
Sakura Wars 3: Is Paris Burning?	Sakura Wars 3 is the third game in the Sakura Wars series. It was made by Red Company and Overworks, published by Sega for the Dreamcast, and released in March 2001. Sega calls it a dramatic adventure game.
Sakura Wars 4 anime scenes	The anime scenes were directed by Susumu Kudo and made by Production I.G. Instead of adding more scenes than past games, the team focused on quality. They mixed hand-drawn animation with computer graphics for smoother motion.
Sakura Wars 4 game system	The game system of Sakura Wars 4 was based on the work done for Is Paris Burning?, with only minimal changes. The story scenario was already finished by the time the game was announced.
Sakura Wars 4 gameplay	The game mixes three styles of play: tactical role-playing, dating sim and visual novel. These parts overlap with each other as you play.
Sakura Wars 4 mecha animation	The computer graphics animation of the mecha in Sakura Wars 4 was made using techniques from the Sakura Wars movie. The team added new video software to make the smoothest play experience yet.
Sakura Wars 4 opening	The opening of Sakura Wars 4 plays on a theme of celebration. It shows the cast in relaxed situations.
Sakura Wars 4 story	The story is set six months after Sakura Wars 3: Is Paris Burning? and Sakura Wars: The Movie. Ichiro Ogami returns to Tokyo and reunites with the Imperial Combat Revue and its Flower Division.
Sakura Wars 4: Fall in Love, Maidens	Sakura Wars 4 is a dramatic adventure game told across three acts. It mixes tactical role-playing, dating sim and visual novel play. You play as Ichiro Ogami, who leads two all-female combat groups.
Sakura Wars battle system	The first Sakura Wars uses turn-based battles on a tilted, grid-based 2D battlefield. Each unit gets two actions per turn, chosen from a list of five.
Sakura Wars gameplay structure	The game is split into adventure segments and battle sections. In adventure segments you explore places and talk with the cast. The choices you make there come into play during battles.
Sakura Wars GB	Sakura Wars GB is a spin-off for the Game Boy Color, set just after the first Sakura Wars. It was made by Jupiter and released by Media Factory in 2000. A direct sequel came out the next year.
Sakura Wars genre	Sakura Wars mixes role-playing, dating sim and visual novel elements. Its marketing called this blend a new genre, "dramatic adventure." Its mix of story and tactical role-playing was inspired by the Fire Emblem series.
Sakura Wars in other media	The Sakura Wars series has grown beyond video games. It has spawned anime, movies, novels, manga and radio dramas.
Sakura Wars live-action shows	Sakura Wars has live-action shows. These shows are focused on the Imperial Combat Revue.
Sakura Wars Makers	Sega made the games, with Red Entertainment handling planning and production. The anime cutscenes come from studios such as Production I.G.
Sakura Wars music	Kohei Tanaka is the composer of the Sakura Wars series. Besides the original soundtracks, many games have inspired orchestral or vocal albums. There are also compilation albums with music from several Sakura Wars games.
Sakura Wars novels and manga	Many Sakura Wars games have been turned into novels and manga. These stories are companion pieces. They offer a take on the game's events or expand the plot with extra scenarios.
Sakura Wars on Sega systems	The Sakura Wars series began on the Sega Saturn, with the first game in 1996 and the second in 1998. The third game, Is Paris Burning?, came out on the Sega Dreamcast in 2001.
Sakura Wars Online	Sakura Wars Online is a Dreamcast game released in 2001. It came with two character packs. One pack is themed after the Tokyo Flower Division, and the other after the Paris Flower Division.
Sakura Wars Other Media	Sakura Wars is more than games. The series also includes anime, manga and stage shows.
Sakura Wars Setting	Sakura Wars is set in a made-up version of Japan's Taisho period. The story takes place in cities like Tokyo and Paris, mixing real places with fantasy events and steampunk-style technology.
Sakura Wars stage shows	Since 1997, the voice actors of Sakura Wars have performed on stage as their characters in live-action musical shows. Some of these stage performances could be seen in the series' other media.

Sarah Bryant's Design	Sarah's ponytail was made to be practical for martial arts, since hair pulling is not allowed in the games. Her longer legs were meant to show that she relies on kick attacks.
Sarah Bryant's Designer	Sarah Bryant was designed by Seiichi Ishii. He said she was inspired by Sarah Connor, a character from the Terminator movies.
Sarah Bryant's Fighting Style	Sarah fights aggressively. She does not stand still waiting for the opponent to move, but moves ahead. Yu Suzuki said this style fully reflects his own personality.

Sarah Bryant's Origin	Sarah Bryant was created during a brainstorming session by the Sega AM2 development team. Her first name was Anego, which showed her role as the sister of Jacky Bryant, who was then called Aniki.
Sarah Bryant's outfit	Sarah's main outfit was made to work as clothing ready for combat. It was also meant to distract her opponents. The outfit has stayed mostly the same across the series, with only small changes.
Sarah Bryant's Second Design	In the second design, Sarah's halter top became a full leotard with a sash. She also had fingerless purple gloves and short dark brown hair.

Saturn hardware team	The Saturn was built by the same team that made the System 32 arcade board. Hideki Sato chose not to base it on the Model 1, worried about leaving behind most developers, who worked with sprites, not 3D.

Scoring tip: opposite elements	Switching to the element opposite an enemy makes the game harder. But it lets you defeat enemies faster and raises your overall score.
Scoring Tips	Shoot an enemy's gun hand to disarm him for extra points with a justice shot. Beat enemies without getting hit or shooting hostages to raise your score multiplier. Shoot background objects, since some reveal power ups.
Scoring Tricks	Your score comes from doing and combining tricks on a BMX bike. A trick is worth more for longer time held, more spinning, and more tricks in a row. Using the same trick often makes it worth less.

Sea Lion	The sea lion is a sea mammal related to seals. Unlike true seals, it has small outer ears and can turn its back flippers forward to walk on land. Sea lions are noisy and often live in large groups.
Sea Otter	The sea otter lives along the coasts of the northern Pacific Ocean. It has very thick fur instead of fat to stay warm. It often floats on its back and uses stones to break open shellfish.
Seahorse	Seahorses are small fish with a head shaped like a horse. They swim upright and hold onto plants with their curled tails. Unusually, the male carries the eggs in a pouch until the young are born.
Seal	The seal is a sea mammal with flippers and a thick layer of fat to stay warm. Seals hunt fish in the water but rest and give birth on land or ice. True seals have no outer ear flaps.

Seaman (video game)	Seaman is a Dreamcast game and one of the few Dreamcast games to use the microphone attachment. The face of the Seaman creature is modeled after the game's producer, Yoot Saito.
Seaman development	Seaman was developed by Vivarium and designed by Yoot Saito. Saito first thought of the idea as a joke when one of his coworkers was making a tropical fish simulator.

Sega	Sega is one of the world's most prolific makers of arcade games. The company is known for its video game consoles, its creativity, and its new ideas.
Sega 32X	The Sega 32X is an add-on made by Sega for the Genesis. It came out in November 1994. Sega did not release a steady flow of games for it. A standalone version called the Sega Neptune was announced but then canceled.
Sega 4x Memory Card	Sega's official 4x Memory Card holds 800 blocks, four times a standard VMU. A button selects one of four pages, and four orange lights show which page is in use. Not all games work with it, so Sega listed incompatible games.
Sega All Stars	Sega All Stars was Sega's budget series for the Dreamcast in North America. It had 17 titles, each selling for $19.95 in the United States and $29.95 in Canada.
Sega All Stars covers	Sega All Stars covers have an orange bar with the brand name written from top to bottom. In Europe, the budget covers use a blue color scheme instead.
Sega All Stars disc labels	Sega All Stars discs have a small circle with the brand printed inside it. Original releases say Sega Dreamcast on the disc, but All Stars versions just say Dreamcast.
Sega All Stars game types	Seven Sega All Stars games were first released as Dreamcast launch titles. Most are rated E for Everyone by the ESRB, and most have a sports theme, though a few do not.
Sega AM2	Sega AM2 is a game studio. It was once known as AM2 of CRI. In 2001 it was renamed SEGA-AM2 Co., Ltd.
Sega AM2 in the late 1990s	In the late 1990s, Yu Suzuki of Sega AM2 focused on the Virtua Fighter series in arcades. He also worked as a producer on other titles.
Sega AM2 palm tree logo	Sega AM2 uses a palm tree logo. Yu Suzuki said in 1996 that the palm tree stands for reliance and peace of mind.
Sega AM3	Sega AM3 is the developer of Crazy Taxi. The game was published by Sega and first came out in arcades in 1999.
Sega AM9	Sega AM9 made Space Channel 5. The team had staff from Team Andromeda, makers of Panzer Dragoon, and from the Sonic the Hedgehog series, plus some newcomers. It grew from ten people to 27 over almost two years.
Sega and Atari	Unhappy with how Tonka handled the Master System, Sega looked for a new US partner through Atari Corporation, led by Jack Tramiel. Tramiel turned the offer down and focused on Atari's computers instead.
Sega and Bandai	In the late 1990s, Sega tried to merge with the toy company Bandai. The merger did not go through.
Sega and JVC	Sega partnered with JVC to make the Sega CD. JVC had been working with Warner New Media on a CD player that used the CD+G standard.
Sega and Nintendo	The term console war became popular in the late 1980s and early 1990s to describe the fight between Sega and Nintendo. Sega was trying to break into the United States market with its Sega Genesis.
Sega and Nintendo rivalry	The 16-bit era was shaped by the rivalry between Sega and Nintendo. Sega made the Mega Drive, called the Genesis in North America. Nintendo made the Super Nintendo Entertainment System, called the Super Famicom in Japan.
Sega and the Dreamcast	While making Space Channel 5: Part 2, the team knew that the Dreamcast would be the last game console made by Sega.
Sega and Tonka	Sega had no North American sales and marketing group of its own. It sold its Master System there through Tonka. Sega was unhappy with how Tonka did, so it looked for a new partner for the Genesis.
Sega Arcade	Sega is one of the biggest makers of arcade games and machines. Its arcade hits include racing, fighting, and gun games. Recent Sega arcade games often run on the NAOMI board, which is similar to the Dreamcast.
Sega arcade business	Sega's arcade business stayed strong in the late 1990s, and its arcade income went up. This happened even though arcades were struggling in the West, as home consoles became more popular than arcades there.
Sega arcade downturn	The arcade business began to slow down in 1982. In September 1983, Gulf and Western sold its North American arcade game making group and the rights to its arcade games to Bally Manufacturing.
Sega Archives from USA	In Japan, the Sega Smash Pack series is called Sega Archives from USA. The first Sega Smash Pack is Vol. 1, Sega Puzzle Pack is Vol. 2, and Sega Smash Pack 2 is Vol. 3.
Sega as a third-party developer	After stopping the Dreamcast, Sega became a third-party developer. It began making games for several different platforms instead of only its own console.
Sega Bass Fishing	Sega Bass Fishing is a fishing game from Sega. It came out in Japan as a dedicated arcade game, and it was in arcades there by early 1998. There is also a version for the Sega Dreamcast.
Sega Bass Fishing 2	Sega Bass Fishing 2 is the sequel to Sega Bass Fishing. It was made by WOW Entertainment and came out for the Sega Dreamcast in 2001.
Sega Bass Fishing 2 controllers	Sega Bass Fishing 2 can be played with the standard Dreamcast controller. However, the game was designed to support the Dreamcast Fishing Controller.
Sega Bass Fishing 2 players	Sega Bass Fishing 2 is a single-player game. It does not include multiplayer play.
Sega Bass Fishing 2 release dates	Sega Bass Fishing 2 came out for the Dreamcast on 21 August 2001 in North America. It was released in Japan on 30 August 2001.
Sega Bass Fishing Connection	Sega Marine Fishing is a direct sequel to Sega Bass Fishing.
Sega Bass Fishing game modes	Sega Bass Fishing has an ARCADE MODE and an ORIGINAL MODE. In ARCADE MODE you can get new lures as you play.
Sega Bass Fishing tournaments	The game has four tournaments: the Amateur Tournament, the Challenge Tournament, the Professional Tournament, and the Masters Classic Tournament. Players try to win first place in each one.
Sega becomes a game maker	Sega imported second-hand machines that often needed repairs. To fix them, Sega began building its own replacement guns and flippers. This step helped Sega move from importer to maker and led it to develop its own games.
Sega Cards	The original Master System models play both cartridges and Sega Cards. Sega Cards are a game format about the size of a credit card.
Sega CD	The Sega CD was an earlier add-on for the Genesis, released in 1991. It did not meet commercial expectations and did not really extend the Genesis lifespan.
Sega CD 2	The Sega CD 2, or Mega-CD 2, came out in Japan on April 23, 1993. It was made to cost less to build, so it is smaller and has no motorized disc tray.
Sega CD 2 in North America	The Sega CD 2 reached North America a few months after its Japan release. It cost US$229 and came with the game Sewer Shark.
Sega CD and full-motion video	Sega of America said the extra storage on Sega CD discs allowed full-motion video, or FMV. Digital Pictures became an important partner for Sega.
Sega CD chips	A custom graphics chip was planned to handle scaling and rotation. The add-on would also have an extra sound chip made by Ricoh.
Sega CD design goals	The add-on was first meant to match the TurboGrafx-CD, but with twice as much RAM. The team also wanted fairly short loading times and arcade-style hardware scaling and rotation, which needed a special digital signal processor.
Sega CD first showings	Sega first showed the system to the public at the 1991 Tokyo Toy Show. It was also shown at the Consumer Electronics Show in Chicago in mid-1991.
Sega CD Game Bundles	The Sega CD was costly, which limited who would buy it. To add value, Sega bundled more games with it in the US and the UK, with some packages including up to five games.
Sega CD games	Well-known Sega CD games include Sonic CD, Lunar: The Silver Star, Lunar: Eternal Blue, Popful Mail, and Snatcher. The library also has many games brought over from the Genesis and many FMV games.
Sega CD hardware	The Sega CD plays games on CDs and adds a faster CPU to the Genesis. It also has a custom graphics chip for better sprite scaling and rotation. It can play audio CDs and CD+G discs too.
Sega CD in Brazil	Tectoy, a Brazilian toy company, released the Sega CD in Brazil in October 1993. It kept the North American name, even though the main console was called Mega Drive there.
Sega CD names	The Sega CD is a CD-ROM add-on for the Sega Genesis. In Japan it is called the Mega-CD. Magazines were already writing about a CD-ROM add-on for the Genesis as early as 1990.
Sega CD North American launch	The Sega CD came out in North America on October 15, 1992, for US$299. It was the North American name for the Mega-CD. Ads used the Sega slogan "Welcome to the Next Level".
Sega CD overheating problem	Before launch, testers found some units bursting into flames. The system used a cheap audio CD drive, not a true CD-ROM drive. Some games jumped between disc tracks too often, which overheated the motors that move the laser.
Sega CD price	Late changes, like the extra CPU and more RAM, raised the estimated cost of the Sega CD to US$370. Sega's market research showed buyers would pay more for a state-of-the-art machine.
Sega CD RAM	Sega raised the Sega CD's RAM from 1 to 6.5 Mbit after rumors that NEC would upgrade the TurboGrafx-CD. At first the RAM was too slow to run programs well, so developers had to work on making it faster.
Sega CD second CPU	The Sega CD has its own extra Motorola 68000 CPU. It was added because the Genesis CPU was too slow for the Sega CD's new graphics. This second CPU runs at 12.5 MHz, faster than the 7.67 MHz CPU in the Genesis.
Sega CD storage	The main plus of CDs was storage space. A CD held about 160 times more data than a Genesis cartridge. This made full-motion video (FMV) games possible, such as the controversial Night Trap.
Sega Challenge	At the end of 1987, Sega teamed up with astronaut Scott Carpenter to start the Sega Challenge. This traveling program in recreational centers tested kids on skills like concentration and learning new skills. It used the games Out Run and Shooting Gallery.
Sega Channel	Sega Channel was a subscription service for the Sega Genesis that delivered games, and local television providers hosted it. It needed special hardware that plugged into both a cable line and the Genesis.
Sega characters in Segagaga	Taro meets many Sega characters, such as Sonic the Hedgehog, Ristar, Alex Kidd, Nei from Phantasy Star 2, Opa-Opa from Fantasy Zone, the Bad Brothers from Golden Axe, and Amigo from Samba de Amigo.
Sega consoles in the late 1990s	In the second half of the 1990s, Sega made the 32X, Saturn, and Dreamcast. These consoles did not do well for Sega. Sony became the top console maker with the PlayStation, and Nintendo was also a rival.
Sega Dreamcast	The Dreamcast is a console made by Sega. It was the first console of the sixth generation and arrived before the PlayStation 2, Xbox, and GameCube.
Sega DVD Distribution System	In June 1999, The Nihon Keizai Shimbun reported that Sega was building a DVD distribution system with Hitachi, Nippon Columbia, and another partner. One plan was encrypted discs holding many titles, unlocked with downloadable product keys.
Sega Enterprises name	In 1965 the company became known as Sega Enterprises, Ltd. This happened after it bought Rosen Enterprises, a company that imported coin-operated games. In 1969 Sega was sold to Gulf and Western Industries.
Sega Enterprises, Ltd.	Sega Enterprises, Ltd. was formed in 1965. Rosen was CEO, Stewart was president, and LeMaire was director of planning. Soon after, Sega stopped leasing to military bases and moved from slot machines to coin-operated amusement machines.
Sega Extreme Sports	Sega Extreme Sports is a sports game made by Innerloop Studios, a game company from Norway. It came out under several different names and was published by many companies.
Sega Extreme Sports in Japan	In Japan, the console version was ported and published by Sega. It was released there on September 6, 2001.
Sega Game Gear	The Game Gear is a handheld game system released by Sega in Japan in 1990. It has a color screen with a backlight, which made it use batteries quickly. With an adapter, it can play Master System games.
Sega Genesis	The Sega Genesis came out in 1988. Sega marketed it as a 16-bit console that was technologically better than its competitors. The 32X was later made as an add-on to extend its life.
Sega Genesis release	The Mega Drive came out in Japan on October 29, 1988. As the Sega Genesis, it launched in New York City and Los Angeles on August 14, 1989, then the rest of North America later that year.
Sega GT	Sega GT is a racing game for the Sega Dreamcast. It came out in Japan and in North America.
Sega GT for Windows	A Microsoft Windows version of Sega GT came out in 2001. Sega published it in Japan, Activision Value in North America, and Empire Interactive in Europe.
Sega GT Homologation Special	Sega GT Homologation Special is the name of the Japanese version of Sega GT on the Dreamcast. It was out in Japan by May 2000.
Sega GT North American version	Sega GT also has a North American version for the Dreamcast. It came after the Japanese version, Sega GT Homologation Special.
Sega Hitmaker	Sega Hitmaker is a division of Sega, the Japanese video game developer. It carries the Hitmaker name as part of Sega.
Sega in the Early 1980s	In the early 1980s, Sega was one of the top five arcade game makers in the United States. At that time it was owned by Gulf+Western.
Sega in the mid-1990s	Sega's revenue fell between 1992 and 1995 during a slowdown across the whole game industry. Money lost on the Saturn added to Sega's money problems.
Sega Joyopolis beta test	Virtua Fighter 3 was tested at the Sega Joyopolis arcade in Tokyo. Players waited in line six to eight hours for one round. At this point the team was fine-tuning move timing and button sensitivity.
Sega leaders in 1984	Rosen stepped down as president of Sega Enterprises, Inc. on January 1, 1984, and Jeffrey Rochlis became president and CEO. After the buyout, CSK head Isao Okawa became chairman and Nakayama became CEO of Sega Enterprises, Ltd.
Sega leaves the console market	After five years of losing money, Sega stopped making console hardware in 2001. Sega then became a third-party company, making and publishing games for other systems.
Sega management buyout	In 1984, Nakayama and Rosen set up a buyout of Sega's Japanese company with money from CSK, a Japanese software company. Their group of investors bought Sega's Japanese assets for $38 million.
Sega Marine Fishing	Sega Marine Fishing is a 2000 fishing game published by Sega for the arcade, Dreamcast, and Windows. The focus is on getting fish to bite the lure, then fighting the fish and reeling it to the boat.
Sega Mark III	The Sega Mark III came out in 1985. It used Sega's arcade hardware inside to give sharper graphics. It was a bit more powerful than the Famicom, and Sega's ads pushed its better graphics.
Sega Master System	The Sega Master System is an 8-bit home video game console made by Sega in the mid-1980s. It competed with the Nintendo Entertainment System. It sold better in Europe and Brazil than in North America.
Sega Mega Anser	The Sega Mega Anser was a peripheral for the Mega Drive in Japan. It worked as an online banking system and an answering machine.
Sega Mega Drive	The Mega Drive is a Sega home console released in Japan in October 1988. Sega built it from its arcade game technology, using 16-bit processor boards.
Sega Model 1	The Model 1 was a Sega arcade system board from 1992 and 1993. It ran Sega AM2's Virtua Racing and Virtua Fighter, which helped make 3D polygon graphics popular. It was expensive to make.
Sega Model 2	Yu Suzuki worked on the Sega Model 2 after the Sega Model 1. He took costly military texture mapping technology from Lockheed Martin and brought it down to $50 per chip, giving the game industry mass-produced texture mapping.
Sega Model 3	Yu Suzuki led the development of the Sega Model 3 arcade hardware. It debuted with Virtua Fighter 3.
Sega Model Arcade Hardware	Yu Suzuki introduced and led the Model series of arcade hardware. It helped lay the base for 3D arcade games at AM2 and at other Sega arcade departments too.
Sega My Card	Sega My Cards are pocket-sized game cards that replaced the original SG-1000 cartridges. Hideki Sato said the old cartridges looked like small black tombstones in the console. He called replacing them his proudest achievement of the SG-1000 era.
Sega Naomi	The Sega Naomi is the upgraded arcade system board counterpart of the Dreamcast. Like the Dreamcast, it is powered by the PowerVR2 graphics chip.
Sega Nomad	The Sega Nomad was the first handheld of the fifth generation of video game consoles. It had a lifespan of just two years and was discontinued before the other handhelds of the era came out.
Sega of America	Sega of America was set up in 1986 to handle Sega's consumer products in North America. Sega hoped its console business would do better there than it had in Japan.
Sega of America after the Tonka deal	After the Tonka deal, much of Sega of America shifted away from marketing and distribution to focus on customer service. During this time, Lowry left the company.
Sega of America and the Sega CD	Sega of America did not learn the project details until mid-1991. It got early technical papers but no working unit to test. Producer Michael Latham said Japan sent dummy units, fearing leaks, which was very frustrating.
Sega of America leaders	Shoichiro Irimajiri replaced Tom Kalinske as chairman and CEO of Sega of America. Bernie Stolar, who used to work at Sony Computer Entertainment of America, became executive vice president for product development and third-party relations.
Sega on Dolphin controllers	Greg Thomas, a Sega of America vice president, said Dolphin's sensory controllers worried him. They were rumored to have microphones and headphone jacks. He saw them as a sign that someone was thinking about something different.
Sega origins	Sega began as Nihon Goraku Bussan. It became known as Sega Enterprises, Ltd. after buying Rosen Enterprises in 1965. Its roots go back to American Standard Games in 1940 and Service Games of Japan in the 1950s.
Sega Patent 6,200,138	In 2001, Sega was awarded U.S. Patent 6,200,138. It describes an arcade cabinet similar to Harley-Davidson & L.A. Riders (1997). It also describes the arrow navigation and pedestrian avoidance used in Crazy Taxi.
Sega Pico	The Sega Pico is an educational game system for young children, released in the early 1990s. Games come as cartridges shaped like picture books, and children use a pen to interact with them.
Sega R&D No. 8	Sonic Team, once called CS3, was renamed Sega Research and Development Department 8, or R&D No. 8. It was also called AM8, though the team made only home console games.
Sega Racing Controller	The Dreamcast version of Sega Rally 2 works with Sega's Racing Controller, a steering wheel add-on. The wheel came out in Japan on 28 January 1999, the same day as the game.
Sega Rally	Sega Rally is a racing series made by Tetsuya Mizuguchi's team at Sega. Mizuguchi gives the credit to his team. He told his staff, "it's your game, not mine!"
Sega Rally 2	Sega Rally 2 is a rally driving game. It came out in arcades and on the Sega Dreamcast. It has arcade-style handling and many courses and game modes.
Sega Rally 2 arcade cabinet	The arcade cabinet was designed by Sega AM4. Its designers tried different frames, seats and speaker setups. They wanted players to feel rally driving through movement, vibration and sound.
Sega Rally 2 arcade hardware	Sega Rally 2 runs on Sega's Model 3 arcade hardware. The first Sega Rally Championship used Model 2. The team used Model 3 to improve the graphics and driving, aiming to recreate World Rally Championship racing.
Sega Rally 2 as a Killer Application	The Italian magazine Consolemania said Sega Rally 2 was the first game Sega planned to use as a "killer application" for the Dreamcast. That means a game meant to make people want to buy the console.
Sega Rally 2 Checkpoint System	Sega Rally 2 uses a checkpoint system in its races, in the style of arcade racing games. Players race over dirt and slide their cars through the turns.
Sega Rally 2 Home Versions	Sega Rally 2 came out on two home platforms, the Dreamcast and the PC. The Dreamcast version is based on the arcade game and has a two-player split screen mode.
Sega Rally 2 music	The soundtrack has original songs and live-recorded music. Composer Jun Senoue recorded the arcade music with live instruments. A soundtrack album came out in Japan on 1 April 1998.
Sega Rally 2 on Dreamcast	The Dreamcast version of Sega Rally 2 has more courses than the arcade version, plus many game modes. In the UK, it was one of the launch games for the Dreamcast, alongside Sonic Adventure.
Sega Rally 2 online play	The Dreamcast version uses Microsoft's Windows CE and DirectX. The Japanese release uses DirectPlay for networked multiplayer. In March 1999, it was the only networked multiplayer game for the Dreamcast in Japan.
Sega Rally 2 Paris Competition	When the Dreamcast launched in Europe in October 1999, a head-to-head Sega Rally 2 competition was held in Paris, France. The winner got a specially branded Dreamcast scooter. The contest was part of the French launch celebrations.
Sega Rally 2 Spanish Advertisement	In Spain, a print ad for the Dreamcast release pointed to the 1998 Rally of Great Britain. It used co-driver Luis Moya's famous plea to Carlos Sainz Sr. to restart his stalled car.
Sega Rally Championship	Sega Rally Championship is a 1995 arcade racing game by Sega. Players drive rally cars over dirt, gravel, and snow, and each surface handles differently. It was later released on the Sega Saturn.
Sega references in Segagaga	Segagaga is packed with nods to Sega and its games, made for Sega fans. The game is very self-aware and often refers to itself and to Sega.
Sega S.A. (Segasa)	Six months after the sale, Martin Bromley and Stewart formed Sega S.A. in Spain. It was also called Segasa and Sega/Sonic. The company brought coin-operated machines into Europe.

SG-1000	The SG-1000 was Sega's first video game console. It came out in Japan on July 15, 1983. That was the same day Nintendo launched its Family Computer, also called the Famicom.
SG-1000 and Master System	When the arcade market fell in the early 1980s, Sega began making home game consoles. The first were the SG-1000 and the Master System. They struggled against rivals like the Nintendo Entertainment System.
SG-1000 and the Famicom	The SG-1000 launched in the same month as Nintendo's Famicom. The Famicom had games like Donkey Kong.
SG-1000 around the world	Sega itself only sold the SG-1000 in Japan, but rebranded versions came out elsewhere, including France, Italy, and Spain. It was not released in the United States, United Kingdom, or Germany.
SG-1000 controller	On the original SG-1000, the controller is wired into the system and cannot be removed. The SG-1000 II has a detachable controller instead.
SG-1000 Controllers	The SJ-200 joystick was attached to the SG-1000, and the SJ-150 joypad was made for the SG-1000 II. The SH-400 racing wheel was made for games like Monaco GP.
SG-1000 family of machines	The SG-1000 series includes the original SG-1000, the SG-1000 II and the Mark III. Sega also made the SC-3000, a home computer model.
SG-1000 game library	The SG-1000 and SC-3000 support 51 ROM cartridge games and 29 Sega My Card games. All SG-1000 games also work fully on the Mark III and the Japanese Master System.
SG-1000 hardware	The SG-1000 uses an 8-bit Zilog Z80A CPU rated for 4 MHz that runs at 3.58 MHz. Its video chip is a Texas Instruments TMS9918A that can show up to 15 colors, and its sound chip is a Texas Instruments SN76489AN.
SG-1000 II	Sega released the SG-1000 II on July 31, 1984. It was a revised version of the SG-1000 with several hardware changes, including controllers that could be detached.
SG-1000 Japan launch	The SG-1000 came out in Japan on July 15, 1983, for 15,000 yen. Nintendo launched its Family Computer, or Famicom, in Japan on the same day.
SG-1000 launch day	The SG-1000 was released in Japan on July 15, 1983. That was the same day Nintendo released its Family Computer in Japan.
SG-1000 launch games	The SG-1000 had three launch games. All of them were ported from Sega's VIC dual-arcade board. By the end of 1983, there were 21 SG-1000 games, compared to only 9 games for the Famicom.
SG-1000 Mark II	Sega redesigned the SG-1000 to try to challenge Nintendo. The SG-1000 Mark II could still play SG-1000 games, but it did not win Sega any more buyers.
SG-1000 memory	The SG-1000 has 1 KB of main RAM and 16 KB of video RAM. Video and audio go out through an RF switch, and power comes from a 9 V DC connector hooked to an AC adapter.
SG-1000 models	The SG-1000 came in several forms. These include the SC-3000 computer and the redesigned SG-1000 II from 1984. The Mark III, released in 1985, added an improved custom video display processor.
SG-1000 video output	The SG-1000 did not have an RCA output for connecting it to a TV.
SGI Pitch to Sega	SGI founder Jim Clark first showed his game chip idea to Tom Kalinske, head of Sega of America, who was impressed. But Sega's engineers in Japan turned it down over technical problems, which SGI later fixed.
SH-1	The SH-1 was the basic SuperH model and supported 56 instructions. It did not support 64-bit multiplication, so the MUL, DMULS and DMULU instructions caused a trap on it.
SH-2	The SH-2 added 64-bit multiplication with MUL, DMULS and DMULU. It also added a few extra commands for branching and other jobs, bringing it to 62 supported instructions.
SH-2 Chip	In 1993, Sega and Hitachi worked together to make a new CPU for the Saturn. The result was the SuperH RISC Engine, also called the SH-2. Sega picked it for its cost and efficiency.
SH-2 in Cars	The SH-2 is used in many car engine control units. Car makers using it include Subaru, Mitsubishi, and Mazda.
SH-2 in Sega Consoles	The SH-2 chip is used in Sega video game hardware. It powers the Sega Saturn console and the Sega 32X add-on.
SH-2 processor	The SH-2 is a 32-bit RISC chip with a 16-bit fixed instruction length for high code density. It has a five-stage pipeline and a hardware multiply-accumulate block for DSP work.
SH-2 registers	The SH-2 provides 16 general-purpose registers. It also has a vector-base register, a global-base register, and a procedure register. All ROM-less SH-2 devices have a cache.
SH-3 byte ordering	The SH-3 is bi-endian. This means it can run in either big-endian or little-endian byte ordering.
SH-3 core	The SH-3 core was added to the SuperH family a few years after earlier cores. It brought a new interrupt concept, a memory management unit (MMU), and a changed cache design. It added six new instructions for a total of 68.
SH-3 processor	The SH-3 is used in mobile and handheld devices such as the Jornada. It is strong in Windows CE applications and in the car navigation market.
SH-3-DSP	SH-3-DSP is a DSP extension of the SH-3 core. It has extended data paths, special accumulators and a dedicated MAC-type DSP engine. It brought the DSP and RISC processor worlds together in one core.
SH-4 and the Dreamcast	In 1997, Hitachi and STMicroelectronics began working together on the SH-4 for the Dreamcast. It can run two instructions at once and has a vector floating-point unit that is well suited to 3D graphics.
SH-4 processor	The SH-4 is used where high performance is needed. It is found in car multimedia terminals, set-top boxes, and video game consoles, most notably the Dreamcast.
SH-4 standard chips	Standard chips based on the SH-4 came out around 1998. The SH-4 was designed by Hitachi and STMicroelectronics.
SH-5 backward compatibility	SH-5 mixes a compact 16-bit instruction encoding with a more powerful 32-bit one. Unlike similar designs, its backward compatibility mode is the 16-bit encoding rather than the 32-bit encoding.
SH-5 mixed instructions	Starting with SH-5, the design includes both 16-bit and 32-bit instructions. The 16-bit ones map onto 32-bit versions inside the CPU, saving memory without needing much extra decoding logic.
SH-5 operating modes	The SH-5 design supports two modes. SHcompact mode matches the user-mode instructions of the SH-4. SHmedia mode is very different, using 32-bit instructions, sixty-four 64-bit integer registers, and SIMD instructions.
SH-5 processor	The SH-5 is part of the SuperH family. It is intended for high-end 64-bit multimedia applications.
SH-DSP and SH-3-DSP	The SH-DSP was first made for mobile phones, then used in consumer products needing DSP power, such as for JPEG compression. The SH-3-DSP is used in multimedia terminals, networking, printers, and fax machines.
Shader system	Quake III Arena uses a shader system for its graphics. The look of many surfaces is defined in text files called shader scripts.

Shenmue features	In Shenmue, people in town follow regular daily schedules. Players can pick up and look closely at detailed objects. The game also uses Quick-time events, where players press buttons as they appear on screen.
