Sonic the Hedgehog (1991 video game)	Sonic the Hedgehog is a fast-paced side-scrolling game released by Sega in 1991 for the Mega Drive, called Genesis in North America. Sonic races through levels to stop Dr. Robotnik and free animals.
Sonic the Hedgehog 2	Sonic the Hedgehog 2 is a game made by Sega in 1992 for the Sega Genesis. It introduced Tails, a fox with two tails who follows Sonic. It also added the spin dash move and Super Sonic.
Sonic the Hedgehog 3	Sonic the Hedgehog 3 is a video game released by Sega in 1994 for the Sega Genesis, also called the Mega Drive. Sonic and Tails face Knuckles the Echidna and Dr. Robotnik. Players can save their progress.
Sonic the Hedgehog character	Sonic is a blue hedgehog designed by artist Naoto Ohshima for an internal Sega mascot contest. He was put into a prototype game by Yuji Naka, and his look was made less aggressive to appeal to more people.
Sonic the Hedgehog Music	The music for the first Sonic the Hedgehog game was written by Masato Nakamura of the band Dreams Come True. Before the game came out, Sega sponsored the band's Wonder 3 tour and painted Sonic on the tour bus.
Sonic the Hedgehog on the Genesis	In the early 1990s, Sega was one of the most successful video game companies thanks to its Genesis console. Genesis sales were driven by Sonic the Hedgehog, Sega's main series of 2D platform games.
Sonic X-treme	Sonic X-treme was a Sega Saturn game made by Sega Technical Institute. It was planned as the first Sonic game with full 3D gameplay, but it had many setbacks and was canceled in 1996.
Sonic's design goals	Sonic was designed so children could draw him easily and find him familiar. He was also meant to show a cool attitude that stood for the United States at the time.
Sonic's English voice in Sonic Adventure	Starting with Sonic Adventure, Ryan Drummond voices Sonic in English.
Sonic's First Appearance	Sonic was first shown in the 1990 arcade racing game Rad Mobile. He was a small ornament hanging from the rearview mirror.
Sonic's First Appearances	Sonic made a cameo in the arcade game Rad Mobile in 1990. He officially debuted in 1991 in Sonic the Hedgehog, a platform game for the Sega Genesis.
Sonic's first voice in Sonic CD	Sonic first had a few voice samples in Sonic CD. Designer Masato Nishimura provided the voice for these samples.
Sonic's Japanese voice in Sonic Adventure	Junichi Kanemaru voices Sonic in Japanese, starting with the release of Sonic Adventure.
Sonic's Original Look	Ohshima's first design made Sonic short and round, with short quills and no visible irises. In Sonic the Hedgehog 2 on the Mega Drive, his head to height ratio changed from 1:2 to 1:2.5.
Sonic's personality	Sonic's personality was based on the 'Get it done' attitude of Bill Clinton, who was Governor of Arkansas when Sonic was made and later became President of the United States.
Sonic's shoes	Sonic's shoes grew from a design inspired by Santa Claus and by Michael Jackson's boots. The red color came from the contrast of colors on Jackson's 1987 album Bad.
Sonic's singing voice in Sonic Underground	In the DiC cartoon Sonic Underground, Sam Vincent provided Sonic's singing voice. Jaleel White voiced Sonic in that show.
Sonic's Speed	Sonic's greatest ability is how fast he can run. He is known as the world's fastest hedgehog.

Sony and the PlayStation	Sony had worked with Nintendo on a CD-ROM add-on for the SNES. When that deal ended, Sony used the work it had done to build what became the PlayStation console.
Sony and Toshiba Chip Venture	On April 1, 1999, Sony and Toshiba set up a joint company in Nagasaki Prefecture to make the Emotion Engine chip. Sony Computer Entertainment holds a 49 per cent stake in this company.
Sony Computer Entertainment	Sony Computer Entertainment is the video game division of the Japanese electronics company Sony. It released the PlayStation console in 1994, which became a huge success. Its follow-up, the PlayStation 2, came out in 2000.
Sony PlayStation	The PlayStation is a home video game console made by Sony and first released in Japan in 1994. It plays games on CDs and has sold tens of millions of units. Its successor, the PlayStation 2, came out in 2000.
Sony restructuring	Shortly after the PlayStation 2 was unveiled, Sony announced a major restructuring. It included cutting jobs and putting more focus on PlayStation as a core part of the company's future.
Sony vs Sega and Nintendo	By the late 1990s, Sony had overtaken its established rivals Sega and Nintendo in the global video game market.
Sony's Goal for the PlayStation 2	Sony wanted a second hit in a row, noting that neither Nintendo nor Sega had won with two consoles back to back. Chris Deering of Sony Computer Entertainment Europe compared it to winning two gold medals at back-to-back Olympics.

Sorcerian	Sorcerian is a fantasy game. Instead of one long adventure, it is split into fifteen separate small quests, which gives the game a good amount of variety.
Sorcerian attributes	Characters in Sorcerian have seven main attributes: strength, intelligence, protection, magic resistance, vitality, dexterity, and karma. Class and job choices affect these attributes in different ways.
Sorcerian characters and party	In Sorcerian the player can create up to ten characters. Up to four of them can be in the party at the same time.
Sorcerian classes and jobs	Characters can be one of four classes or races: fighter, wizard, elf, or dwarf. There are over 60 jobs, from clown to exorcist. Each choice has its own strengths, weaknesses, and equipment limits.
Sorcerian English version music	Sierra Entertainment made the English version of Sorcerian. Rob Atesalp and Ken Allen turned the original music into an arrangement that works with the MT-32 MIDI sound device.
Sorcerian Expansion Packs	The PC-8801 version of Sorcerian got add-on packs with new scenarios. Falcom made some, such as Sengoku Sorcerian and Pyramid Sorcerian. Amorphous made the Selected Sorcerian packs, and Quasar Soft made Gilgamesh Sorcerian.
Sorcerian Forever	Sorcerian Forever is a version of Sorcerian made by Falcom. It came out in 1997 for PCs running Microsoft Windows.
Sorcerian gameplay style	The action in Sorcerian is arcade in style, which is typical for a Japanese game. It is not just hack-and-slash, because there are puzzles to solve along the way.
Sorcerian magic	Sorcerian has a magic system that players use during their adventures, alongside the arcade-style action.
Sorcerian monsters	Sorcerian is known for its gigantic monsters. Enemies include a hydra boss and many dragons.
Sorcerian music composers	The music for the original Sorcerian was written by Yuzo Koshiro, Mieko Ishikawa, Reiko Takebayashi, Hideya Nagata, and Takahito Abe. The music for the Additional Scenarios made by Falcom was done by Mieko Ishikawa alone.
Sorcerian on Consoles	Sorcerian was made for consoles, with content somewhat different from the PC versions. Sega made the Mega Drive version, and Victor Musical Industries made the PC Engine CD version.
Sorcerian on PC Engine CD	Sorcerian came out on the PC Engine CD. For this version, Kenji Kawai arranged the music from the original game.
Sorcerian Original	Sorcerian Original is a remake of Sorcerian made by Falcom. It came out in 2000 for PCs running Windows.
Sorcerian party control and puzzles	The player controls the whole party at once. Members run in a line, jump one after another, and attack together, like the Options in Gradius. Some puzzles need a certain class, such as a strong character to force open doors.
Sorcerian scenarios	Sorcerian has fifteen scenarios, or quests, that the player can play in any order. The party must fight enemies and do tasks in each scenario's levels to clear it before picking another.
Sorcerian Super Arrange Version	This is a set of three albums arranged by Hiroyuki Namba. Volume 1 covers the base scenario. Volume 2 adds Additional Scenario Vol. 1, and Volume 3 covers Additional Scenario Vol. 2 and Vol. 3.
Sorcerian: Shichisei Mahou no Shito	Sorcerian: Shichisei Mahou no Shito is the Dreamcast version of Sorcerian. It was developed by Exe-Create and Media JuGGLer, and its content differs somewhat from the PC versions.

Soul Edge (the weapon)	Soul Edge is a legendary weapon that the story of Soulcalibur centers on. It is held by a warrior named Nightmare, who kills countless people to feed the blade's bloodlust.
Soul Fighter	Soul Fighter is a 3D beat 'em up game for the Sega Dreamcast, released in 1999. It was made by the French company Toka and published by TLC Multimedia. Fighting is based on martial arts styles and a small set of weapons.
Soul Fighter heroes	There are three heroes in Soul Fighter. Altus is a fearless warrior, Sayomi is a female spy, and Orion is a powerful wizard. They escaped the curse that changed the other villagers.
Soul Fighter story	Queen Antea has cast an evil spell on the Kingdom of Gomar. A strange mist covers the land and turns the people into vicious creatures. Three heroes who escaped must find and capture souls to undo the curse.
Soul Reaver on Dreamcast	A Dreamcast version of Soul Reaver came out in 2000. It was made by Nixxes Software, and it was the first project that Nixxes ever worked on.
Soul Reaver story setting	Soul Reaver takes place 1500 years after the events of Blood Omen. It follows the journey of Raziel, a vampire who becomes a wraith.
Soulcalibur	Soulcalibur is a fighting arcade game released by Namco in 1998. It runs on Namco's System 12 hardware. It is the sequel to Soul Edge, which came out three years earlier.
Soulcalibur Arcade Hardware	The arcade version of Soulcalibur ran on Namco System 12 hardware, which is based on the PlayStation. The Dreamcast version added new features and better graphics, and it ran even better than the arcade game.
Soulcalibur arcade release	Soulcalibur first came out in Japanese arcades on July 30, 1998. Releases in North America and Europe followed later the same year.
Soulcalibur arcade version	Soulcalibur was first announced in January as New Weapon Fighting Game, and a test version was shown at E3 in May. About sixty people made the arcade version on Namco's System 12 hardware.
Soulcalibur character motions	Characters were made to look like real people. Motion creator Masataka Ishiguro stressed arm and leg movements tied to each weapon, so players could feel each motion and the realism of the game.
Soulcalibur Dreamcast character faces	For the Dreamcast version, Namco refined the faces and animations of the fighters. They changed facial proportions and modeled details like the inside of the mouth and the jaw so the characters show better expressions.
Soulcalibur Dreamcast lighting	The Dreamcast version of Soulcalibur uses real-time lighting effects. These make character shadows look better and improve how skin looks under torchlight. The team also made the motion-capture data more precise.
Soulcalibur Dreamcast stages	The Dreamcast version of Soulcalibur shows all of its stages in full 3D polygons. In the arcade original, the far backgrounds were flat, two-dimensional images. This was the biggest technical change in the home version.
Soulcalibur fighting styles	Each character's fighting style is built around their weapon. Because the weapons are so different, the team found it hard to balance the game.
Soulcalibur game concept	Yotoriyama said the idea of Soulcalibur was to show fun and diversity in weapon combat. Each weapon changes how the game plays and how it reacts when it clashes with another weapon.
Soulcalibur game modes	Soulcalibur has several modes of play, including Arcade Mode, Time Attack Mode, Extra Survival Mode and Practice Mode. There is also a Museum with different areas to explore.
Soulcalibur Gameplay	Soulcalibur puts a heavy focus on fighting with weapons. Namco made it working closely with its Tekken team. Its free eight-way movement adds more strategy to each fight.
Soulcalibur Mission Battle mode	The Dreamcast version of Soulcalibur has an expanded Mission Battle mode. Namco added extra content to give the game replay value, based on research into other fighting games sold at the time.
Soulcalibur movement and ring out	Soulcalibur gives players more freedom of movement than Tekken 3, making fights more tactical. This movement ties closely into the game's ring out feature.
Soulcalibur name	The game was named Soulcalibur to avoid trouble with Edge Games. That company claimed it had the sole right to use the word edge in games when Namco tried to trademark the name Soul Edge outside Japan.
Soulcalibur new fighters	Soulcalibur adds ten new fighters: Astaroth, Edge Master, Inferno, Ivy, Kilik, Lizardman, Maxi, Nightmare, Xianghua, and Yoshimitsu.

Street Fighter Alpha 3 on PlayStation	Street Fighter Alpha 3 came to the PlayStation in 1998. This version used hit polygons instead of hit sprites, so more memory could go to character animations.
Street Fighter Alpha 3 PlayStation Version	In the PlayStation version, Balrog, Juli and Juni can be played right away. It also adds Dee Jay, Fei Long and T. Hawk from Super Street Fighter II, plus Guile, Evil Ryu and Shin Akuma.
Street Fighter Alpha 3 Story	The story takes place two years after Street Fighter Alpha 2. Various World Warriors track down M. Bison and his Doomsday Device, the Psycho Drive. Each character has their own storyline, with rivals in the fifth and ninth matches.
Street Fighter Alpha 3: Saikyo Dojo	Street Fighter Alpha 3: Saikyo Dojo is the 1999 Dreamcast version of the game. In Japan it is called Street Fighter Zero 3: Saikyo-ryu Dojo. It has all the added features of the PlayStation version, but a different World Tour mode.
Street Fighter Alpha attack buttons	The buttons are light, medium, and hard. Light attacks are faster but weaker, hard attacks are stronger but slower, and medium attacks fall in between.
Street Fighter Alpha matches	Each battle is a best-of-three rounds match. Both health bars start full each round, and emptying the other bar wins the round. Winning two rounds wins the match and moves you to the next opponent.
Street Fighter Alpha players and controls	One player can fight the computer, or two players can fight each other at the same time. Each player uses an 8-way joystick and 6 buttons.
Street Fighter Collection	Street Fighter Collection for the PlayStation and Sega Saturn includes Super Turbo. Super Street Fighter II is on the same disc, and Street Fighter Alpha 2 Gold is on a second disc.
Street Fighter II	Street Fighter II is a fighting game made by Capcom, first released in arcades in 1991. Players choose from several fighters, each with special moves. Its huge success started a wave of fighting games in the 1990s.
Street Fighter II attack buttons	The buttons are marked L, M, and H for light, medium, and hard. Light attacks are faster but weaker, hard attacks are stronger but slower, and medium attacks fall in between.
Street Fighter II forward and backward	Moves are given as forward and backward, not left and right. When your fighter faces right, right is forward and left is backward. When facing left, this flips.
Street Fighter II losing and continuing	If a single player loses to the computer, the game is over. The player must continue to rematch the opponent who just beat them.
Street Fighter II players and controls	One player can fight the computer, or two players can fight each other at the same time. Each player has an 8-way joystick and 6 buttons.
Street Fighter II rounds and matches	Each match is best of three rounds, and both health bars start full each round. Empty your foe's health bar to win a round. Win two rounds to win the match and face the next opponent.
Street Fighter II starting position	Player one always starts each fight on the left side, facing right. Move directions in the guide assume your fighter is facing right.
Street Fighter II story	M. Bison, ruler of the Shadaloo crime syndicate based in Thailand, sponsors the second Street Fighting tournament. The first tournament ended when Ryu beat the champion Sagat with a Shoryuken uppercut across his chest.
Street Fighter II: Air Attacks	To attack from the air, jump straight up or jump diagonally. Then press any single attack button while your fighter is in mid-air.
Street Fighter II: Crouching Block	Hold the joystick diagonally down and back to block while crouching. This stops low and middle attacks, and high attacks usually go over your head. It does not stop air attacks.
Street Fighter II: Standing and Crouching Attacks	To attack while standing, press any single attack button. To attack while crouching, pull the joystick down, including either down diagonal, and press any single attack button.
Street Fighter II: Standing Block	Push back on the joystick when the opponent attacks to block. A standing block stops middle, high, and air attacks, but not low attacks. Pressing back with no attack coming just moves you away.
Street Fighter II: Winning a Round	To win a round, you use your fighter's attack moves to damage the opponent. You must also block or dodge the opponent's attacks.
Street Fighter III	Street Fighter III is a 1997 fighting game by Capcom, first released as a coin-operated arcade game. It is the sequel to Street Fighter II. It uses the CD-ROM-based CP System III hardware.
Street Fighter III announcement	Capcom announced Street Fighter III on March 27, 1996, at a meeting in Tokyo. Capcom said the game took more than two years to make. Work on it started in 1994.
Street Fighter III Attack Buttons	The buttons are light, medium, and hard. Light attacks are weaker but faster. Hard attacks are stronger but slower, and medium attacks fall in between.
Street Fighter III blocking	To block, hold the joystick away from your opponent, and hold back and down to block low attacks. Special moves and Super Arts cause small block damage. Some attacks are unblockable, and you cannot block in mid-air.
Street Fighter III Cast	The developers of Street Fighter III chose to focus on a mostly original cast. Characters from Street Fighter II, such as Ken and Chun-Li, were considered at first. Ken was added to the roster later in development.
Street Fighter III character designs	Yasuda worked on the character designs for Street Fighter III. He tried to stay within the design limits set by Sadamoto. In earlier games, Yasuda had made the design choices more directly himself.
Street Fighter III dashing	All characters can dash forwards and backwards. A dash quickly moves the character several character lengths, making it a great way to move into or out of an opponent's range.
Street Fighter III Double K.O.	If both fighters knock each other out at once, it is a double K.O. and both get a win. If each had already lost a round, they fight another round.
Street Fighter III fight timer	During a fight, a timer counts down from 99 to 0, which takes about one minute. If time runs out, the player with the most life wins the round.
Street Fighter III Forward and Backward	Moves are described as forward and backward, not left and right. When your fighter faces right, right is forward and left is backward. When facing left, it is the other way around.
Street Fighter III Judgment	If the timer runs out and both players have the same health, a Judgment occurs. The CPU picks the winner using three judges chosen at random.
Street Fighter III Music Style	The music in the Street Fighter III games is mostly drum and bass. Some songs also mix in jazz, hip-hop and techno.
Street Fighter III parry tips	Timing is key, since tapping too early or too late makes the parry fail. Some unblockable attacks can still be parried. Against a combo, you must keep parrying each hit until it ends.
Street Fighter III parrying	Parrying is new to the series. Tap forward just before an attack hits, or tap down for low attacks. A good parry makes you flash blue, works in mid-air, and lets you counter faster than blocking.
Street Fighter III Players and Controls	One player can fight the computer, or two players can fight each other at the same time. Each player uses an 8-way joystick and 6 buttons.
Street Fighter III Rounds and Matches	Each match is best of three rounds. Both health bars start full each round, and the first to empty the other's bar wins the round. Winning two rounds wins the match.
Street Fighter III Soundtrack CD	The soundtrack for the first Street Fighter III game came out on CD in 1997. It was released by First Smile Entertainment.
Street Fighter III Starting Position	Player one starts every fight on the left side, facing right. Move directions in the guide assume your fighter is facing right.
Street Fighter III: 2nd Impact	Street Fighter III: 2nd Impact is a 1997 arcade fighting game made by Capcom. It is an update of Street Fighter III: New Generation and runs on the CP System III hardware.
Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike	Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike is a 1999 fighting game made by Capcom for arcades. It is the second and final updated version of Street Fighter III, following 2nd Impact, and runs on CP System III hardware.
Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike for Dreamcast	The Dreamcast version of 3rd Strike came out in 2000. It has Arcade, Versus, Training and Options modes, plus a System Direction mode that lets you change several game features.
Street Fighter III: Double Impact	Street Fighter III: Double Impact is a compilation game made only for the Sega Dreamcast. In Japan it is called Street Fighter III: W Impact. It was the first arcade pixel accurate port of the new Street Fighter series.
Street Fighter Zero 3 Upper	Street Fighter Zero 3 Upper is the Dreamcast version of SFA3 ported back to the arcade in Japan. It brings the bigger Dreamcast roster to arcades.
Street Levels	Street levels come in two kinds. In the first, you tag every graffiti point a rival gang tagged before time runs out, while dodging the authorities. The second is a boss battle where you chase rival gang members and spray graffiti on them.
Street Parade in Zurich	While traveling in Europe in 1997, Mizuguchi was taken to the Street Parade in Zurich. It had a large electronic dance music concert with around 300,000 people. The sights and sounds there helped inspire Rez.
Street Puzzle Mode	Street Puzzle is a challenge mode in the home console versions of Puzzle Fighter. In it, you must defeat specific characters to unlock bonus content.
Street Race and Championship	A Street Race is a single race against several opponents. A Championship is four races against three opponents, with points given for your finishing place in each race. It is usually the last challenge in a Chapter.
Streets of Rage	Streets of Rage is a 1991 Sega fighting game for the Mega Drive. Former police officers Axel, Blaze, and Adam battle street gangs to stop a crime boss called Mr. X. A special attack calls in a police car.
Streets of Rage 2	Streets of Rage 2 is a 1992 Sega fighting game for the Mega Drive. Axel and Blaze return, joined by the wrestler Max and Adam's younger brother Skate. They set out to rescue Adam from Mr. X.
Streets of Rage 3	Streets of Rage 3 is a Sega fighting game for the Mega Drive. In Japan it is called Bare Knuckle III. The heroes battle Mr. X again, who now uses robots, and they are joined by a scientist named Dr. Zan.
Streets of Rage Remake	There is no official game called Streets of Rage Remake. Streets of Rage is a series of three beat-em-up games made by Sega for the Mega Drive. In them, fighters clean up a city run by a crime boss.
Strider Hiryu	Hiryu is a Super A Grade Strider, a group of ninja-like secret agents. His main weapon is the Cypher, a plasma broadsword with a tonfa-like handle. Robot helpers sometimes assist him.
Strike Gunner S.T.G	Strike Gunner S.T.G is a game made by Athena. It came out in arcades in 1991 and on the Super NES in 1992.
Striker Match	Striker Match lets a fourth character jump in to help your fighter. You use Strike Bombs to call the Striker, and you can refill them by losing rounds or taunting the other player.
Striker System	The main idea of The King of Fighters 2000 is a bigger Striker System. Strikers are support characters who help the fighters in battle. SNK made the old system broader and deeper instead of changing how people play.
Striker System Removed	Eolith took out the Striker System used in the NESTS games. KOF 2002 goes back to the original system. Older games in the series let players call assistants, but this one does not.
Strikers	KOF '99 adds an assisting character called a Striker. Players can call their Striker in to attack. Bars at the bottom of the screen show how many Strikers the player can still use.
Strikers in The King of Fighters 2000	Many regular fighters from past King of Fighters games are not playable in this game. To make up for it, SNK used the striker system so players can pick helpers like Goro Daimon to assist them in battle.
Strikers Strike Back novel	Strikers Strike Back is a light novel by series writer Akihiko Ureshino, published by Kadokawa Shoten. Released on February 19, 2001, it pokes fun at the game's own story.
Strongman	Strongman is slow and clumsy but has a huge amount of health. He sends out a wave of lava you can jump over with good timing, and he hits with his heavy arm. His big frame makes him an easy target.
Strudel	Strudel is a pastry made of very thin layers of dough rolled around a filling. It is popular in Austria and Germany. Apple strudel, filled with apples, sugar, cinnamon, and raisins, is the best known kind.
Stryfe	Stryfe is a clone of Cable who became a madman. As a grown up, Cable returned to his own time to deal with Stryfe, and he often time travels whenever the need arises.
Stuart Scott commentary	Stuart Scott supplies the color commentary in ESPN NBA 2Night, talking about the action as you play.
Stubborn	Being stubborn means refusing to change your mind or do what others want. Stubborn people hold tightly to their ideas. Mules are often called stubborn animals.
Student B and Student C	Student B and Student C are two boys at Chitose's school, each with a letter on his forehead. They follow Fumitsuki with a video camera and make sarcastic comments, often breaking the fourth wall.
Studio 128	Studio 128 was a more private place where Yu Suzuki's team moved to work. The games After Burner and Power Drift were made there.
Studio Mebius	Studio Mebius is the brand that made Snow. Before Snow, it was known for dark and graphic adult games, so Snow was a change of direction for the brand.
Studying Overseas	After he recovered, Keitaro decided to study overseas with Noriyasu Seta. As he was about to leave, Naru confessed her feelings to him at the airport and chose to wait for his return.
Stuffed tiger	Past the door behind the bookshelf in Chief Irons' office is a stuffed tiger. Its description reads "A stuffed animal". Follow the hallway past it and go through the next door.
Stump	Stumps are fast, annoying enemies known by their bark. They bite up close, spit fire from far away, leap to bite and dodge melee attacks. They are low on health and small, so you can jump over them when cornered.
Stump fire underwater	Jumping into the water will not protect you from a Stump's fire spits. Fire projectiles deal full damage even underwater, so do not hide there.
Stunning Sharks	The sound of Ecco's sonar stuns sharks. While a shark is stunned, Ecco can attack it head-on with his attack.
Stunt Arena	The Stunt Arena is a small area with 20 stars to collect. It has a loop, ramps and a half pipe, and some stars need faster cars to reach. Collecting all 20 stars unlocks a new game mode.
Stunt GP	Stunt GP is a radio-controlled car racing game made by the UK studio Team17. It came out in 2001 for Windows, Dreamcast and PlayStation 2. It uses the RenderWare engine and supports split-screen multiplayer.
Stunt GP publishers	Stunt GP was announced by Team17 and Hasbro Interactive in November 1999. In March 2001, EON Digital Entertainment picked up the rights to publish the PC and Dreamcast versions.
Stunt Mode	Besides racing, the game has a stunt mode. In stunt mode, players perform dirt bike tricks.
Stunt wings	Stunt wings are a feature added to the 3D home versions of San Francisco Rush 2049. They let players glide and do moves in the air. The arcade version does not have stunt wings.
Stunts and Bonus Money	In Crazy Taxi you can earn extra money by doing stunts along the way. One kind of stunt is a near miss, where you drive very close to other cars without hitting them.
Stupid Invaders	Stupid Invaders is a 2000 adventure game from Ubisoft Entertainment, made by Xilam Animation. It plays on Windows 95 and 98 computers and on Mac OS computers, and it comes on more than one CD.
Stupid Invaders cursor controls	On Windows and Mac OS you move the cursor with the mouse. On Dreamcast you use the analog thumb pad or the D-Pad. The cursor changes its look based on what you point at and what your alien can do.
Stupid Invaders cursor icons	A pointing hand means walk, a hand holding an eyeball means look, and a hand with outstretched fingers means take. A hand holding a joystick means use, and a side-viewed hand with outstretched fingers means talk.
Stupid Invaders Dreamcast main menu	The Dreamcast main menu has four options. Use the analog thumb pad or D-Pad to move the cursor to one, then press a button to confirm it.
Stupid Invaders Dreamcast saving	To save and load on Dreamcast, put a VMU in the controller's first expansion slot. Without one, you must finish the game in one sitting and start over from the beginning after a game over.
Stupid Invaders Dreamcast sound setting	The Dreamcast version has a mono/stereo setting in place of a colour setting.
Stupid Invaders Dreamcast title screen	In the Sega Dreamcast version, the Ubisoft and Xilam logos and the opening cutscene play first. Then the title screen appears with PRESS START BUTTON flashing. Pressing Start takes you to the main menu.
Stupid Invaders inventory	Your alien can carry up to six items. After taking something, the cursor looks like the item, and a right click puts it in the inventory. Items can be used on background objects or combined with each other.
Stupid Invaders main menu	The main menu shows Bud holding a plunger, and the mouse cursor looks like a foot. The four options are Play, Load Game, Settings and Quit. An option's letters split up when the cursor is over it, then you click to choose.
Stupid Invaders on Dreamcast	Stupid Invaders also came out on the Dreamcast in 2001. The Dreamcast version was made by Titanium Studios.
Stupid Invaders opening cutscene	After the Ubisoft and Xilam logos and the game's name, the opening cutscene starts. It shows the aliens' spaceship crash-landing on Earth, and the aliens decide to hide in an abandoned house.
Stupid Invaders Quit and Credits options	The Quit option returns you to the title screen. Pressing all five controller buttons at once does the same. Some Dreamcast copies replace Quit with a Credits option, which shows the credits without finishing the game.
Stupid Invaders saving and settings	Load Game lets you load one of up to 27 saved games. Settings lets you change the volume, the subtitles and the colour settings.
Stupid Invaders settings (Dreamcast)	In the Dreamcast version of Stupid Invaders, you push a button and select "Settings" to change options. It has a mono/stereo sound setting instead of the colour setting found on Windows and Mac OS.
Stupid Invaders settings (PC and Mac)	In the Windows and Mac OS versions of Stupid Invaders, you push a key to change the settings. These settings let you change the volume, subtitles and colour.
Stupid Invaders voice cast	The game uses the voice actors from the English version of the cartoon. Charlie Adler voices Candy H. Caramella, Maurice LaMarche voices Etno Polino, and Danny Mann voices Gorgious Klatoo.
Stupid Invaders: Coffin Zombie Tip	Use the claw on a coffin to reveal a zombie holding a key. Use the funnel on the zombie, then the sulphuric acid on the funnel. The zombie wakes, throws the funnel away and melts, and Bud takes the key.
Stupid Invaders: conveyor belt and escalator	From the bottom of the hole, walk Bud left onto a conveyor belt. It carries him to an upward-moving escalator that takes him to the top.
Stupid Invaders: freeing Bud's friends	Go through the left door into the room with four escape pods holding Bud's friends. Use the control pad under the portrait of Dr. Sakarin to open all four pods and free them.
Stupid Invaders: Funnel and Claw	The funnel and claw are on the shelves at the back of the Abandoned House room. Bud uses the claw to pry open a coffin and puts the funnel in the zombie's mouth.
Stupid Invaders: Padlocked Doors	After getting the key, Bud walks back to the shelves, goes up some stairs and climbs a ladder to a padlocked pair of doors. Use the key on the padlock to unlock them.
Stupid Invaders: second tap in The Desert	In The Desert, walk Bud to a second tap and use the hose pipe on it. Bud will connect the hose pipe to the tap.
Stupid Invaders: Sulphuric Acid	In the Abandoned House, Bud must take a can of sulphuric acid. He says the stuff should do the trick. Later he pours it into a funnel placed in a zombie's mouth.
Stupid Invaders: The Abandoned House	The Abandoned House is a part of the game Stupid Invaders. The strategy guide for this part includes lines of spoken dialogue from the game.
Stupid Invaders: The Desert	The Desert is a part of Stupid Invaders where Bud must find his way across hot ground. He walks between screens, picks up items such as a hose pipe and a skull, and uses them to move forward.
Stupid Invaders: The Dung Factory	The Dung Factory is a part of the game Stupid Invaders. In it, the player guides the character Candy through the area.
Stupid Invaders: the optional door at the bottom of the hole	At the bottom of the hole, Bud can walk up through a door if you wish. He gets beaten up by an unseen person inside, then comes back out. This step is not required.
Stupid Invaders: using the skull on the hose pipe	After connecting the hose pipe, use the skull on it. Bud uses the skull to bite off the end of the hose, then holds onto it as he jumps into a hole and drops to the bottom.
Stupid Invaders: Vaporised Santa	In the Abandoned House, Bud can talk to the vaporised Santa after landing. Santa says: "Thank you little boy for saving me and ruining Christmas for everyone else." Talking to him is optional.
Sturgeon	Sturgeons are large, ancient fish with bony plates instead of scales. They live in the rivers, lakes, and seas of the Northern Hemisphere. Their eggs are sold as caviar, and overfishing has made many kinds rare.
Style Kudos and Drifting	Style Kudos come from drifting, using the handbrake to skid through a turn. A K symbol shows while you drift and gets brighter the longer and bigger the drift. A more solid symbol means more Kudos.
Subaru	Subaru is a new character added in the Dreamcast version of Comic Party. She does not appear in the original 1999 Windows game.
Submarine Stage	The submarine level has its own unique items and fixtures. Players can use turrets, small airplanes that drop bombs, and icebergs to throw at opponents.
Success	Success is the company that distributed Psyvariar 2, a vertically scrolling shoot 'em up made by SKONEC Entertainment.
Successor to the Master System	Sega's console team began work on a successor to the Master System almost right after that console came out. Masami Ishikawa led the team, and Hideki Sato supervised it.
Suchie-Pai anime	There is an anime OVA based on the Suchie-Pai mahjong game.
Suchie-Pai character designs	The character designs for the Suchie-Pai series were done by Kenichi Sonoda.
Sucre	Sucre is the official capital of Bolivia and home to its supreme court. The government itself works mainly from La Paz. Sucre is known for its white colonial buildings.
Sudden Death	When the time runs out, the water level rises on each turn. This drowns worms at the lowest points of the map. A drowned worm leaves no headstone.
Suez Canal	The Suez Canal is a waterway in Egypt that links the Mediterranean Sea and the Red Sea. It opened in 1869. Ships use it to travel between Europe and Asia without sailing around Africa.
Suffix	A suffix is a group of letters added to the end of a word. It can change the meaning or the part of speech, as when -ness turns kind into kindness.
Sugiura	Sugiura is a middle-aged man who helps Marufuji and the main character. He is later killed in the main world, likely by a monster that slipped in.
Suika	Suika is a visual novel made by the studio Circus. It is the fourth project from Circus and the second from its Northern group. It came out on July 27, 2001, on CD-ROM for Windows and has adult content.
Suika CD-ROM Editions	Suika came out on CD-ROM in two versions. There was a limited edition and a regular edition.
Suika DVD-ROM release	After the CD-ROM version, Suika was also released for Windows on DVD-ROM. This DVD-ROM release came out on August 31, 2001.
Suika DVD-ROM version	A DVD-ROM version of Suika came out on August 31, 2001. It has several technical improvements over the first CD-ROM release from July 27, 2001.
Suika ending theme	The ending theme is "Fragment: Thought to Wish to the Starlit Sky." Miwa Kozuki sings it in the Windows version. Rino sings it in the PlayStation and Dreamcast versions.
Suika gameplay	Suika follows a linear plot line. It offers set scenarios and set ways for the player to interact, and it focuses on the appeal of the main female characters.
Suika light novel	A light novel based on Suika was published by Paradigm in November 2001. It covers the story from the fourth chapter of the game.
Suika light novel artists	The Suika light novel has illustrations by Takanon Ikuta. Its cover illustration was drawn by Naru Nanao. The book came out in November 2001.
Suika limited edition	Both the CD-ROM and DVD-ROM versions came in a limited edition and a regular edition. The limited edition adds an arranged soundtrack album and a calendar, and the DVD-ROM limited edition also has a T-shirt. Regular editions have no extras.
Suika opening theme	The opening theme is "Fragment: The Heat Haze of Summer." Kamin sings it in the Windows version. Yozuca* sings it in the PlayStation and Dreamcast versions.
Suika opening theme maxi single	Circus released a maxi single on July 15, 2001. It has the opening theme "Fragment: The Heat Haze of Summer" sung by Kamin.
Suika remix album	First Smile Entertainment released a Suika remix album on December 19, 2001.
Suika staff	Mikage led the planning and wrote the story with Ichiro Go. Naru Nanao and Takanon Ikuta shared the art direction and character design. Takanori did the programming.
Suika theme music	Suika has two theme songs, one opening theme and one ending theme. This is true for the Windows version and for the PlayStation and Dreamcast versions. Both songs were written and composed by Tororo.
Sukiyaki	Sukiyaki is a Japanese hot pot dish. Thin slices of beef are cooked at the table with tofu, vegetables, and noodles in a sweet soy sauce broth. Pieces are often dipped in raw beaten egg before eating.
Sumer	Sumer was an early civilization in southern Mesopotamia. The Sumerians built some of the first cities, such as Ur and Uruk, and invented cuneiform, one of the oldest known forms of writing.
Summer scenario	Summer opens after the three heroine plot lines are completed. The player takes the role of Ryuya. Summer is a linear arc, and no choices are given to the player.
Summoning Creatures	When Bayonetta summons creatures to attack her enemies, she loses partial control of her hair. Because her hair goes into the attack, she ends up in more comfortable attire.
Sumo	Sumo is a form of wrestling from Japan. Two large wrestlers try to push each other out of a round ring or make the other touch the ground with anything but the soles of the feet. It has many old traditions.
Sun	The Sun is the star at the center of our solar system. It is a huge ball of hot gas, mostly hydrogen and helium. Its energy comes from nuclear fusion and gives Earth light and heat.
Sun Puyo	Sun Puyo appear in the Game Boy Color version of Puyo Puyo~n. Whenever you counter garbage, Sun Puyo fall onto the field.
Sundog	A sundog is a bright spot of light that appears to one or both sides of the sun. It is caused by sunlight bending through ice crystals in the air. Sundogs often show faint rainbow colors.
Sunfish	The ocean sunfish is the heaviest bony fish in the world and can weigh over a ton. It has a flat, round body that looks like a giant head with fins. It feeds mostly on jellyfish.
Sunlight	Sunlight is the light and heat that reach Earth from the Sun. It takes about eight minutes to travel to Earth. Plants use sunlight to make food, and its ultraviolet rays can cause sunburn.
Sunset Bridge	Sunset Bridge is a place named in Chapter 1 of The Typing of the Dead. Your partners say they will try to meet up with you there later, while you look for further clues.
Suomi	Suomi loves ice skating and was chosen for Finland's figure skating team. After a leg injury, she almost quits, but meeting a young skater named Haruto helps her hope to return and keep her childhood promise with Hanna Janinen.
Super Art Gauge	The Super Art gauge fills as you hit the opponent with regular and special moves. You can only use a Super Art when it is full. Its length and how many you can store depend on which Super Art you chose.
Super Arts	Super Arts are powerful special moves. After you pick a character, you choose one of three Super Arts made just for that character. You can also cancel a special move into a Super Art.
Super Arts Gauge	Each Super Art has its own gauge length and number of stocks. Stronger moves tend to have longer gauges and fewer stocks. Stored power carries over between rounds, but not to fights against a new opponent.
Super Bowling	Super Bowling is an Athena game. It was released on the Super NES in 1992 and on the Nintendo 64 in 1999.
Super Combo Gauge	Every character except Akuma has a Super Combo gauge. It grows as you attack and get attacked. When it is full, you can use a unique and powerful super special move.
Super Combo Gauge Plus (Street Fighter Alpha 3)	Super Combo Gauge Plus, also called Gauge Plus, makes your Super Gauge slowly rise on its own. It also doubles the gauge you gain from attacking and blocking.
Super Combo Levels in A-ism	In A-ism, the level of a Super Combo is set by the strength of the attack button you press. For example, Medium Punch or Kick gives a Level 2 Super Combo. It no longer depends on how many buttons you push.
Super Combos	Super Street Fighter II Turbo introduced Super Combos. After filling the Super meter, a player can perform an automatic combo with many hits that deals a large amount of damage. Ryu's Super Combo is the Shinku Hadoken.
Super Combos and Air Combos	Super Street Fighter II Turbo added new gameplay mechanics. These include combination moves called super combos, and air combos.
Super Desperation Moves	Some desperation moves become Super Desperation Moves if done while your life bar is flashing and your energy bar is full, or with POWer activated in Extra Mode. They deal more damage than any other move in the game.
Super Dimension Macross Japanese title	The Japanese title of The Super Dimension Macross is Cho Jiku Yosai Makurosu. In English it is also called The Super Dimension Fortress Macross.
Super Exp Gain code	The Super Exp Gain code in Gauntlet Legends multiplies the experience you gain. It works out to about one level for each enemy you kill.
Super Exp Gain code bugs	The Super Exp Gain code in Gauntlet Legends is a bit buggy. For some unknown reason, it can cause the game to freeze.
Super Famicom	The Super Famicom is a 16-bit home game console made by Nintendo and released in Japan in 1990. It was sold in other regions as the Super Nintendo Entertainment System. It was a very successful console.
Super Famicom and Super NES release dates	Nintendo released the Super Famicom in Japan on November 21, 1990. It came to North America as the Super Nintendo Entertainment System on August 23, 1991, and to Europe and Australia in April 1992.
Super Fire Pro Wrestling X Premium	Super Fire Pro Wrestling X Premium is a game in the series for the Super Famicom. Fans made an unofficial English translation of it that can be played through console emulators.
Super Gam*Boy in Korea	Samsung handled sales and distribution of the Mega Drive in Korea, where it was named Super Gam*Boy. It kept the Mega Drive logo next to the Samsung name. It was later renamed Super Aladdin Boy.
Super Game Boy	The Super Game Boy was a Nintendo adapter for the SNES. It let players show Game Boy games on a TV in color.
Super Guard and Auto Guard (Street Fighter Alpha 3)	Super Guard means you take no damage when you guard against Special or Super Moves. Auto Guard makes you block attacks automatically as long as you are not attacking.
Super Hang-On	Super Hang-On is a 1987 Sega arcade motorcycle racing game and the sequel to Hang-On. Players race against the clock on courses set on different continents. It was later released on home systems, including the Sega Mega Drive.
Super Jump	Press Down, then quickly Up-Back, Up, or Up-Forward to Super Jump that way. Super Jumps go a little higher than normal jumps, are much quicker, and leave an afterimage of the character.
Super Jump and Double Jump	Frogger can use a super jump to reach higher platforms. After a super jump, he can also do a double jump, which helps clear platforms that have short gaps in front of them.

SuperH	SuperH, or SH, is a 32-bit RISC instruction set architecture developed by Hitachi. It is used in microcontrollers and microprocessors for embedded systems.
SuperH 16-bit instructions	SuperH is notable for using fixed-length 16-bit instructions even though it is a 32-bit architecture. This gives better memory and processor cache efficiency, but means a smaller register file and mostly two-operand instructions.
SuperH and ARM Thumb	ARM processors have a 16-bit Thumb mode that pairs compact instructions with a 32-bit encoding. ARM licensed several patents from SuperH for Thumb. MIPS processors have a similar MIPS-16 mode.
SuperH Code Density	SuperH has high code density compared to other 32-bit RISC designs such as ARM or MIPS. This helps cache and memory bandwidth performance.
SuperH origins	Hitachi first developed the SuperH processor core family in the early 1990s. The idea was one instruction set that would be upward compatible across a series of CPU cores.
SuperH single instruction set	Hitachi made one instruction set for the whole SuperH line. If a chip did not have hardware support for an instruction, running that instruction caused a trap instead.
SuperH Software Support	SuperH has compiler and operating system support. Systems that run on it include Linux, Windows Embedded, and QNX.
SuperH, Inc.	In early 2001, Hitachi and STMicroelectronics formed SuperH, Inc. It plans to license the SH-4 core to other companies and is working on SH-5, the first 64-bit SuperH design. The SH-1 through SH-3 stay with Hitachi.

VMU Memory	The VMU has 128 KB of flash memory. By default 28 KB is kept for system use, leaving 100 KB for saves. This space is split into 200 blocks, and each block is 512 bytes.

Xbox	The Xbox is a video game console from Microsoft. It has the strong financial backing of Microsoft behind it.
Xbox and GameCube announcements	Microsoft and Nintendo announced the Xbox and GameCube in late 2000. After this, some people thought the Dreamcast was outdated, only two years after it came out.
Xbox CPU choice	During prototyping, Microsoft worked with AMD on the Xbox CPU. Just before the January 2001 reveal, Microsoft engineers switched to an Intel CPU, and AMD had not been told before the reveal.
Xbox design leaders	Rick Thompson and Robert J. Bach oversaw the design of the Xbox. Early on, the DirectX team built prototype consoles by buying several Dell computers and using their internal parts.
Xbox Ethernet port	The Xbox uses Ethernet instead of only dial-up networking, which was a debated choice. The Xbox leads said that, with the planned Xbox Live service, it would help friends keep playing together after school or college, even across the country.
Xbox Hard Disk and Internet	The Xbox is the first console with a built-in hard disk. It also has a built-in Ethernet port, so it can connect to the internet over broadband.
Xbox Hardware	Most earlier consoles used specially designed parts, but the Xbox is built from standard PC parts. It has an Intel Pentium III CPU and a graphics chip based on the Nvidia GeForce 3.
Xbox manufacturing	Flextronics helped Microsoft revise the Xbox design and mass produce it, building a factory in Guadalajara, Mexico. Early units had a failure rate of about 25 percent, which Flextronics repaired. Later hardware designs worked to eliminate these failures.
Xbox name origin	The name Xbox came from "DirectX Box", which referred to the system relying on DirectX. The name was quickly shortened to "Xbox" in an e-mail conversation. The development team ended up favoring it.
Xbox origins	In 1998, four engineers from the Microsoft DirectX team began planning a new game console. They were Kevin Bachus, Seamus Blackley, Ted Hase and team leader Otto Berkes. The console would run on Microsoft DirectX technology.
Xbox software	The Xbox runs on Windows 2000 with DirectX 8.1. This makes it easy for PC game makers to start making games for it. It also gives the console more processing power than most other home consoles.

Zeal	Zeal is a demon who appears at the start of Chapter 1. He warns you to stay away from investigating the disappearance of G.
Zeal and Kuarl rematch	Soon after you start driving, Zeal crashes your windshield. He says Goldman gave him a second chance. The fight is identical to the first: six long phrases for Kuarl, then three of Zeal's countdown attacks.
Zebra	The zebra is a wild animal related to the horse. It lives in Africa and has black and white stripes. Each zebra has its own stripe pattern. Zebras live in herds and eat grass.
Zed Two	Zed Two is a small independent game company formed by brothers Ste and John Pickford. They left Software Creations in the mid-1990s because they were unhappy there. They wanted to re-learn game design from the very basics.
Zeebo	No game system or product called Zeebo is known. There is no reliable information about it.
Zelkin	Zelkin was once an enemy of the Star Gladiators. In Plasma Sword: Nightmare of Bilstein, he joins them as a new ally on their quest to destroy Bilstein and the Fourth Empire.
Zelkin Fiskekrogen	Zelkin feels remorse for having fought for the Fourth Empire before. He sets off to Planet Zeta to team up with Hayato and his friends to take on Bilstein and repay what he feels is his debt.
Zelos, the Silver Gigas	Inside Soltis, Ramirez merges with the Silver Gigas Zelos, letting it awaken. Vyse and his crew defeat Zelos from the Delphinus. Then a chunk of Zelos, merged with and controlling Ramirez, lands on the deck for one last fight.
Zeon Reborn and Legitimate Zeon	Garma leads the Zeon Reborn faction and Kycillia leads the Legitimate Zeon faction. Both factions are unique to Blood of Zeon.
Zepp Tokyo	Zepp Tokyo is a music hall in Japan. It hosted the Dance Dance Revolution 2ndMix tournament on September 26, 1999.
Zera	Zera reveals that Valmar won the battle against Granas, who was killed. He plans to use the pieces inside Elena to bring Valmar back to life, and takes her to the Moon of Valmar.
Zero	Zero is a NESTS agent made to contrast with Krizalid, the boss of The King of Fighters '99. Krizalid had a darker personality than Zero.
Zero Cannon	The Zero Cannon is a space-based satellite weapon. Zero fires a powerful energy blast from it at Earth, destroying most of South Town. After Zero is defeated, Heidern or Kula's group destroys the Cannon, depending on the route taken.
Zero Gunner 2	Zero Gunner 2 is a 3D multidirectional shooter made by Psikyo. It is the sequel to the arcade game Zero Gunner. It came out for the Dreamcast in Japan in 2001.
Zeus (Altered Beast)	In the Sega game Altered Beast, the god Zeus raises a fallen warrior from his grave. He sends the warrior to rescue his daughter Athena from an evil lord. The warrior can change into strong beasts during the fight.
Zheng He	Zheng He was a Chinese admiral of the Ming dynasty. In the early 1400s he led seven great voyages with huge fleets. His ships sailed across the Indian Ocean as far as Arabia and East Africa.
Zidane	Zidane is one of the football stars in European Super League. His player model even copies the bald patch on his head.
Zip drive	The Zip drive is a removable disk drive made by Iomega, introduced in 1994. Its disks first held 100 megabytes, far more than a floppy disk. It is widely used for backups and moving files.
Zip lines and levers	Neo can grab onto zip lines by using the opposite colored magnetic field. Levers work the other way, since he pushes them by using the same colored magnetic field.
Zip your lip	Zip your lip is an informal English saying. It means be quiet or keep a secret. It compares closing the mouth to closing a zipper.
Zodiac	The zodiac is a band of twelve constellations along the path the Sun seems to follow across the sky in a year. They include Aries, Leo, and Scorpius. The zodiac is also used in astrology.
Zolt	Zolt is the leader of the rebellion that started after Emperor Regilio died. He took over the lands of every Emperor-elector except Archbishop Milange, so the empire was close to falling.
Zombie alligator	The zombie alligator is a new enemy met in Chapter 4: Despair. It crawls on the ground, walls and even the ceiling, and it takes two hits to destroy.
Zombie barricade in the Outer City	A barricade with many zombies behind it may fall once you pass the wooden crate or near the gate. Wait for the zombies to reach the explosive barrels, then shoot the barrels to take out almost all of them.
Zombie Revenge	Zombie Revenge is a 1999 beat 'em up game made by Sega AM1 and Data East and published by Sega for arcades. A Dreamcast version came out the same year. Players clear a city full of zombies using fists and weapons.
Zombie Revenge and The House of the Dead	Zombie Revenge is a spin-off of The House of the Dead. It has many links to the first game. The zombies look and sound the same as they did in the first House of the Dead.
Zork	Zork is a text adventure game first created at MIT in the late 1970s. Players type commands to explore the Great Underground Empire and collect treasures. It was sold for home computers by Infocom and led to several sequels.
Zorndyke	Zorndyke is a character in Blue Submarine No. 6, the anime OVA based on a 1967 manga.
Zorndyke's Admiral	The Admiral of Zorndyke's navy is very prone to fits of anger and jealousy. He wants his Papa's approval and seeks it by killing humans. He wrongly believes humans make his Papa sad, not the wars.
Zurg's ion blaster attacks	Emperor Zurg fires yellow ion balls and homing green ion balls. These shots can distract and hurt Buzz, so watch out for them and dodge them during the fight.
ZX Spectrum	The ZX Spectrum is a home computer released by Sinclair Research in Britain in 1982. It was cheap, small, and had rubber keys. It was very popular in Britain and helped start many British game companies.
